Key Findings
The California election has entered its final stretch, with the governor’s race at the top of the ticket and 52 House races that will help determine the party in control of the 120th Congress. The November 3 ballot also includes 14 state propositions—five legislative measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—the most since the November 2016 election. The 2025–26 legislative session ended in late August with a flurry of bills sent to Governor Newsom to sign or veto in September. The recent trends in job growth, consumer prices, and interest rates send mixed signals about the US and California economy.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey on topics including the November races, legislative ballot measures, and citizens’ initiatives, as well as state and national issues that was conducted September 4–September 10, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) continues to lead Steve Hilton (R) by a wide margin (60% to 38%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a similarly wide margin (62% to 36%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty-five percent say that the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote. Fifty-eight percent say that voting is more important this year than in past midterms. After reading the ballot titles and labels, majorities would vote yes on Proposition 1 (55%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (60%; Rainy Day Fund). Three other legislative ballot measures fall short of a majority.
Fifty-two percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would also vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (61%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (55%; Immunology Bond), Proposition 41 (51%; Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), and Proposition 42 (54%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Partisans vary in their support for these citizens’ initiatives. Three other citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Overwhelming majorities agree that there are too many propositions on the state ballot.
Majorities of adults and likely voters think that the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Fifty-one percent of adults and likely voters say that they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance, while 45 percent of adults and 48 percent of likely voters approve of the state legislature. Majorities of adults and likely voters report that recent price increases have caused financial hardships for their household. Seventy percent of Californians think that the state is divided into economic groups, the haves and have-nots. Majorities of adults and likely voters say that they can trust the state government in Sacramento to do what is right “only some of the time.”
Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-three percent of adults and 27 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance, while 17 percent of adults and 16 percent of likely voters approve of the US Congress. Seven in ten Californians are dissatisfied with the availability of affordable health care and believe that the US government is responsible for ensuring that all Americans have access to health care. Fewer than half say the major parties have a lot or some good ideas. Overwhelming majorities say they can trust the federal government to do what is right “only some of the time.”
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
The top two vote-getters in the California June primary for statewide elected offices and for federal and state legislative seats are on the November ballot. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom, who is termed out of office. There are 52 House races in California that will help determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will also decide on 14 state propositions this fall—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax measures and multibillion-dollar state bonds.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a wide margin (60% to 38%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. In our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/), Becerra led Hilton by 25 points (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 93 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 92 percent of Republicans favor Hilton, while independents lean toward the Democratic candidate (57% Becerra, 38% Hilton). Majorities favor Becerra over Hilton across age, education, gender, homeownership, and income groups and in the state’s major regions except for the Central Valley (46% Becerra, 52% Hilton).
Affordability and the cost of living have been the top issue on Californians’ minds in our recent polling. Sixty-five percent of likely voters say that the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote (30% somewhat, 5% not too important). In our February survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/), the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability were very important to 61 percent of likely voters and to majorities across parties, regions, and demographic groups. Today, majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions hold this view. Notably, partisans are largely in agreement: 69 percent of Democrats, 65 percent of Republicans, and 59 percent of independents say that the gubernatorial candidates’ affordability positions are very important. Becerra supporters (66%) express this opinion as often as Hilton supporters (65%). Seven in ten or more of those who live in the Inland Empire (79%) or Los Angeles (70%), those who have incomes of $40,000 to $99,999 (74%), those who have children 18 or younger in their household (74%), Latinos (71%), renters (70%), and women (70%) say the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote.
Many Californians are watching news about the gubernatorial candidates. About six in ten likely voters say they are following news about candidates for the governor’s election either very (18%) or fairly (40%) closely. By comparison, in our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten likely voters were very (23%) or fairly closely (48%) following the news about candidates in the governor’s election, including majorities across partisan groups (68% Democrats, 76% Republicans, 65% independents) and demographic groups and regions. Similar shares were closely following the news about candidates in the gubernatorial election in September 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2018/) (21% very, 41% fairly), while fewer were in September 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2022/) (17% very, 33% fairly), and overwhelming majorities were in September 2021 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2021/) (40% very, 41% fairly) prior to the special election on the recall of Governor Newsom. Today, partisans vary in following the news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely (57% Democrats, 68% Republicans, 50% independents), as do Becerra and Hilton supporters (53% to 69%).
House Races. When asked about their House district race, most likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a wide margin (62% to 36%). Likely voter preferences were similar in July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican) and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, likely voters’ preferences for the Democratic candidate and the Republican candidate are similar in the governor’s race and the House race. More than nine in ten Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while independents say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (59% to 36%). Majorities say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district races across demographic groups and major state regions with the exception of the Central Valley (47%).
Many Californians believe that their vote matters in the 2026 midterm election. When asked about the importance of voting this year compared to past midterm elections, 58 percent of likely voters say it is more important, 39 percent say it is about as important as in past years, and only 2 percent say voting is less important to them. Californians are more likely to say that voting in the midterm is more important to them this year than they were in September 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2022/) (43%) and in September 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2018/) (52%). Today, Democratic likely voters (69%) are much more likely than Republicans (50%) and independents (45%) to say that voting in this midterm is more important this year. Majorities across the state’s regions say that voting in this midterm election is more important this year. Those who say they would vote for Democratic candidates (64%) are more likely than those supporting Republican candidates (49%) in their local House races to say that voting is more important to them this year than in past midterms.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We also gauged support for five state propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Fifty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute that authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 43 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (75% Democrats, 19% Republicans, 56% independents) and between homeowners and renters (49% to 72%). Half or more across the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that increases the state’s rainy day fund, approved by voters in 2014 to provide funding for economic downturns; 39 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (82% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 60% independents). Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 2 across age, education, gender, homeownership, and income groups and the state’s major regions.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-two percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute that repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 53 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (55% Democrats, 19% Republicans, 41% independents). Half or more would vote no across the state’s major regions.
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Thirty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment; 59 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 5 falls short of a majority across partisan groups (40% Democrats, 34% Republicans, 28% independents) and across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . Forty-three percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that increases the percentage of voters needed to approve local special taxes from a majority to two-thirds; 51 percent would vote no. Support varies across partisan groups (33% Democrats, 61% Republicans, 43% independents) and state regions (60% Central Valley; 50% Orange/San Diego; 43% Los Angeles; 35% Inland Empire; 32% San Francisco Bay Area).
When we asked likely voters which of the 14 state propositions they are most interested in, 9 percent chose one of the five legislative ballot measures (5% Proposition 1; 1% Proposition 2; 1% Proposition 4; 1% Proposition 5; 1% Proposition 43). https://timesofsandiego.com/politics/2026/10/27/gen-z-has-very-different-views-on-taxes-than-boomers-but-one-generation-votes-more-often/
# Gen Z has very different views on taxes than Boomers, but one generation votes more often
An age gap exists across the top issues on California’s ballot this November: youth overwhelmingly favor taxing billionaires and not requiring IDs to vote, while seniors would prefer to block new taxes and impose voter ID requirements.
...
They make up 30% of the state’s adult population but only 21% of its likely voters; adults age 55 and older, meanwhile, represent 36% of Californian adults but nearly 50% of expected voters, according to the research organization.
...
## SD in DC
### Gen Z voters are largely against Voter ID
Proposition 39, which would require citizens to present government-issued identification to vote, has been championed by its proponents as a “common-sense constitutional amendment.”
...
Students wait in line to vote on Proposition 50 at the Price Center at UC San Diego on Nov. 4, 2025.
(Photo by Ariana Drehsler/CalMatters)
Only 27% of likely voters age 18 to 29 support Prop.
39, as opposed to 46% of voters age 50 to 64, according to the polling conducted by the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies.

Proposition 39 , also known as the California voter ID initiative , is an initiated constitutional amendment (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initiated_constitutional_amendment) in the state of California (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California) that on November 3, 2026, will be on the ballot. The initiative would amend the state constitution (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_California) to require the use of a government-issued ID for in-person voting, as well as the last four digits of a unique government-issued ID number when casting a mail-in ballot (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mail-in_ballot).
The amendment would also require the state of California to provide free voter ID cards that can be used to cast a ballot, and would enforce the maintenance of accurate voter registration lists by the secretary of state (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_secretary_of_state) and election officials. If approved, the amendment would make California the 37th U.S. state to require voter ID during elections, and the 10th U.S. state to support a voter ID ballot measure.
Background
[ edit (https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2026_California_Proposition_39&action=edit&section=1) ]
Currently, the state constitution (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_California) limits voting to U.S. citizens (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._citizens), though proof of citizenship (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_of_citizenship) is not required unless a voter has become a U.S. citizen less than 15 days before an election. During the voter registration process, individuals must provide a form of ID and attest that they are a U.S. citizen under penalty of perjury (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perjury). [ 1 ] California is one of only 14 U.S. states that does not require identification while voting on election day (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Election_Day_(United_States)). [ 2 ]
On April 24, 2026, state officials announced that the initiative had qualified for the November ballot after supporters submitted over 1.3 million signatures. [ 3 ] [ 4 ] [ 5 ]
Three other states – Nevada (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Nevada_Question_7), North Carolina (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_North_Carolina_Require_Voter_Identification_Amendment), and Oklahoma (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma) – will also see voter ID measures on their November 2026 ballots. [ 6 ]
Impact
[ edit (https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2026_California_Proposition_39&action=edit&section=2) ]
The initiative would amend the state constitution to enforce the use of government-issued ID while voting in-person, and the use of the last four digits of a government-issued ID number when voting by mail (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mail-in_ballot). [ 3 ] Additionally, it would mandate the maintenance of accurate voter registration lists by the secretary of state (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_secretary_of_state) and county election officials, and require the state of California to provide free ID cards upon request to voters casting a ballot. [ 3 ]
The voter ID initiative would also authorize the California legislature (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_legislature) to enact laws that would force compliance with the amendment, and permit citizens to seek judicial review if they feel the state of California or any county within it is failing to comply with the amendment. [ 7 ] Additionally, the state auditor (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_Auditor) would be required to publicly audit state and county compliance every second year. [ 7 ]

Proposition 39 , also known as the California voter ID initiative , is an initiated constitutional amendment (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initiated_constitutional_amendment) in the state of California (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California) that on November 3, 2026, will be on the ballot. The initiative would amend the state constitution (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_California) to require the use of a government-issued ID for in-person voting, as well as the last four digits of a unique government-issued ID number when casting a mail-in ballot (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mail-in_ballot).
The amendment would also require the state of California to provide free voter ID cards that can be used to cast a ballot, and would enforce the maintenance of accurate voter registration lists by the secretary of state (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_secretary_of_state) and election officials. If approved, the amendment would make California the 37th U.S. state to require voter ID during elections, and the 10th U.S. state to support a voter ID ballot measure.
Background
[ edit (https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2026_California_Proposition_39&action=edit&section=1) ]
Currently, the state constitution (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_California) limits voting to U.S. citizens (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._citizens), though proof of citizenship (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_of_citizenship) is not required unless a voter has become a U.S. citizen less than 15 days before an election. During the voter registration process, individuals must provide a form of ID and attest that they are a U.S. citizen under penalty of perjury (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perjury). [ 1 ] California is one of only 14 U.S. states that does not require identification while voting on election day (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Election_Day_(United_States)). [ 2 ]
On April 24, 2026, state officials announced that the initiative had qualified for the November ballot after supporters submitted over 1.3 million signatures. [ 3 ] [ 4 ] [ 5 ]
Three other states – Nevada (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Nevada_Question_7), North Carolina (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_North_Carolina_Require_Voter_Identification_Amendment), and Oklahoma (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma) – will also see voter ID measures on their November 2026 ballots. [ 6 ]
Impact
[ edit (https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2026_California_Proposition_39&action=edit&section=2) ]
The initiative would amend the state constitution to enforce the use of government-issued ID while voting in-person, and the use of the last four digits of a government-issued ID number when voting by mail (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mail-in_ballot). [ 3 ] Additionally, it would mandate the maintenance of accurate voter registration lists by the secretary of state (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_secretary_of_state) and county election officials, and require the state of California to provide free ID cards upon request to voters casting a ballot. [ 3 ]
The voter ID initiative would also authorize the California legislature (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_legislature) to enact laws that would force compliance with the amendment, and permit citizens to seek judicial review if they feel the state of California or any county within it is failing to comply with the amendment. [ 7 ] Additionally, the state auditor (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_Auditor) would be required to publicly audit state and county compliance every second year. [ 7 ]

Proposition 39 , also known as the California voter ID initiative , is an initiated constitutional amendment (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initiated_constitutional_amendment) in the state of California (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California) that on November 3, 2026, will be on the ballot. The initiative would amend the state constitution (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_California) to require the use of a government-issued ID for in-person voting, as well as the last four digits of a unique government-issued ID number when casting a mail-in ballot (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mail-in_ballot).
The amendment would also require the state of California to provide free voter ID cards that can be used to cast a ballot, and would enforce the maintenance of accurate voter registration lists by the secretary of state (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_secretary_of_state) and election officials. If approved, the amendment would make California the 37th U.S. state to require voter ID during elections, and the 10th U.S. state to support a voter ID ballot measure.
Background
[ edit (https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2026_California_Proposition_39&action=edit&section=1) ]
Currently, the state constitution (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_California) limits voting to U.S. citizens (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._citizens), though proof of citizenship (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_of_citizenship) is not required unless a voter has become a U.S. citizen less than 15 days before an election. During the voter registration process, individuals must provide a form of ID and attest that they are a U.S. citizen under penalty of perjury (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perjury). [ 1 ] California is one of only 14 U.S. states that does not require identification while voting on election day (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Election_Day_(United_States)). [ 2 ]
On April 24, 2026, state officials announced that the initiative had qualified for the November ballot after supporters submitted over 1.3 million signatures. [ 3 ] [ 4 ] [ 5 ]
Three other states – Nevada (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Nevada_Question_7), North Carolina (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_North_Carolina_Require_Voter_Identification_Amendment), and Oklahoma (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma) – will also see voter ID measures on their November 2026 ballots. [ 6 ]
Impact
[ edit (https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2026_California_Proposition_39&action=edit&section=2) ]
The initiative would amend the state constitution to enforce the use of government-issued ID while voting in-person, and the use of the last four digits of a government-issued ID number when voting by mail (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mail-in_ballot). [ 3 ] Additionally, it would mandate the maintenance of accurate voter registration lists by the secretary of state (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_secretary_of_state) and county election officials, and require the state of California to provide free ID cards upon request to voters casting a ballot. [ 3 ]
The voter ID initiative would also authorize the California legislature (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_legislature) to enact laws that would force compliance with the amendment, and permit citizens to seek judicial review if they feel the state of California or any county within it is failing to comply with the amendment. [ 7 ] Additionally, the state auditor (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_Auditor) would be required to publicly audit state and county compliance every second year. [ 7 ]

Proposition 39 , also known as the California voter ID initiative , is an initiated constitutional amendment (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initiated_constitutional_amendment) in the state of California (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California) that on November 3, 2026, will be on the ballot. The initiative would amend the state constitution (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_California) to require the use of a government-issued ID for in-person voting, as well as the last four digits of a unique government-issued ID number when casting a mail-in ballot (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mail-in_ballot).
The amendment would also require the state of California to provide free voter ID cards that can be used to cast a ballot, and would enforce the maintenance of accurate voter registration lists by the secretary of state (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_secretary_of_state) and election officials. If approved, the amendment would make California the 37th U.S. state to require voter ID during elections, and the 10th U.S. state to support a voter ID ballot measure.
Background
[ edit (https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2026_California_Proposition_39&action=edit&section=1) ]
Currently, the state constitution (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_California) limits voting to U.S. citizens (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._citizens), though proof of citizenship (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_of_citizenship) is not required unless a voter has become a U.S. citizen less than 15 days before an election. During the voter registration process, individuals must provide a form of ID and attest that they are a U.S. citizen under penalty of perjury (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perjury). [ 1 ] California is one of only 14 U.S. states that does not require identification while voting on election day (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Election_Day_(United_States)). [ 2 ]
On April 24, 2026, state officials announced that the initiative had qualified for the November ballot after supporters submitted over 1.3 million signatures. [ 3 ] [ 4 ] [ 5 ]
Three other states – Nevada (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Nevada_Question_7), North Carolina (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_North_Carolina_Require_Voter_Identification_Amendment), and Oklahoma (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma) – will also see voter ID measures on their November 2026 ballots. [ 6 ]
Impact
[ edit (https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2026_California_Proposition_39&action=edit&section=2) ]
The initiative would amend the state constitution to enforce the use of government-issued ID while voting in-person, and the use of the last four digits of a government-issued ID number when voting by mail (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mail-in_ballot). [ 3 ] Additionally, it would mandate the maintenance of accurate voter registration lists by the secretary of state (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_secretary_of_state) and county election officials, and require the state of California to provide free ID cards upon request to voters casting a ballot. [ 3 ]
The voter ID initiative would also authorize the California legislature (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_legislature) to enact laws that would force compliance with the amendment, and permit citizens to seek judicial review if they feel the state of California or any county within it is failing to comply with the amendment. [ 7 ] Additionally, the state auditor (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_Auditor) would be required to publicly audit state and county compliance every second year. [ 7 ]

California Prop 39: What the voter ID measure may change & where it fits in the national battle
LAist's Jill Replogle shares what she’s learned from the author of Prop 39, its opponents and election experts.
This initiative would change California’s constitution to require voters to provide a government-issued ID when they cast a ballot. Mail-in voters would have to include the last four digits of their ID on the ballot envelope. The measure would also require election officials to use “best efforts,” using government data to verify that voters on registration rolls are U.S. citizens, and to report annually the percentage verified.
What’s at stake?
Voter ID. This would be a big change from how voting currently works in California.
Right now, election officials verify a voter’s identity when they register to vote. They also verify that the signature on a voter’s mail-in ballot matches the signature in their voter registration file.
But voters do not have to provide ID every time they cast a ballot.
Prop. 39 would change that and require voters to present a government-issued ID every time they vote.
The initiative would also shrink the long list of documents (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/regulations/hava_id_regs_from_barclays_3_3_06.pdf) the state currently accepts as proof of identity and residency for voting purposes. If Prop. 39 passes, only government-issued IDs, such as a driver’s license, passport, or state ID card, would be accepted.
The measure would require California to offer free state ID cards to eligible voters who lack another type of government-issued ID.
Official title on the ballot: Prop. 39: Prohibits citizens from voting unless they present government-issued identification
Language you will see: (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/index.htm)
Invalidates mail ballots that do not have last four digits of designated government-issued identification number written on envelope. Prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Fiscal Impact: Costs of between tens of millions of dollars and low hundreds of millions of dollars each year to implement new voting requirements.
What your vote means
A "yes" vote means: Voters would be required to present additional identifying information to elections officials each time they vote.
A "no" vote means: A voter’s identity would continue to be established with the voter’s signature.

Understanding Prop. 39
Currently, when someone registers to vote in California, they do not have to provide proof of citizenship. Rather, they have to check a box on their registration form attesting to being a U.S. citizen and California resident.
Lying on that form is a crime (perjury) punishable by fines and jail time.
Prop. 39 wouldn’t change that process.
What it would do is require election officials to make “best efforts” to verify the citizenship of people on voter registration rolls by cross-referencing their information against government data.
Why now?
According to a recent UC Berkeley poll (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/8hv8929c), just 22% of California Republicans surveyed have confidence in the election system, compared to 88% of Democrats. The two Republican legislators who proposed Prop. 39 see it as a step toward remedying that distrust.
President Donald Trump has also increasingly cast doubt on the integrity of elections across the U.S., including the claim that large numbers of noncitizens are voting. Efforts to find and prosecute noncitizen voters have thus far turned up few culprits (https://www.propublica.org/article/noncitizen-voting-trump-homeland-security-investigations).
But there have been a handful of recent cases in the news of noncitizens registering to vote, including a Honduran green card-holder who was charged with voter fraud (https://www.justice.gov/usao-cdca/pr/honduran-national-living-san-fernando-valley-arrested-federal-criminal-complaint) in August. Last year, an election integrity activist in Orange County was charged with fraud for registering and voting for her dog (https://laist.com/news/politics/dog-registered-to-vote-orange-county-redistricting-fight).
Here’s what supporters say
Supporters of Prop. 39 say requiring voter ID is a common sense reform to increase trust in the electoral process while maintaining voter conveniences including mail-in ballots. Supporters note that polling has found widespread support (https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2025/08/22/majority-of-americans-continue-to-back-expanded-early-voting-voting-by-mail-voter-id/) for voter ID across political parties. They also say using a voter’s signature on their mail-in ballot to verify identity, as California currently does, delays election results and causes some valid voters to have their ballots rejected.
Notable supporters: California Republican Party, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, Republican gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton, U.S. Congressman Ken Calvert (CA-41), Republican state Senator. Tony Strickland (Huntington Beach), Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (San Diego).
Here’s what opponents say
Opponents of Prop. 39 note that documented voter fraud is extremely rare (https://electionfraud.heritage.org/). They say the initiative feeds into Trump’s false claims of widespread election fraud, and would unfairly shut out eligible voters who make simple mistakes, like mixing up their ID number when writing it on their ballot envelope. They also say the federal government’s current system for verifying state voters’ eligibility is prone to error (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/watch-out-false-voter-fraud-claims-fueled-save-program).
Notable opposition: California Democratic Party, UCLA Voting Rights Project, U.S. Senator Alex Padilla, California Labor Federation
Potential financial impact
The state Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates that implementing Prop. 39 could cost anywhere from tens of millions to several hundred million dollars. Read the full analysis here (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=39&year=2026).

California Prop 39: What the voter ID measure may change & where it fits in the national battle
LAist's Jill Replogle shares what she’s learned from the author of Prop 39, its opponents and election experts.
This initiative would change California’s constitution to require voters to provide a government-issued ID when they cast a ballot. Mail-in voters would have to include the last four digits of their ID on the ballot envelope. The measure would also require election officials to use “best efforts,” using government data to verify that voters on registration rolls are U.S. citizens, and to report annually the percentage verified.
What’s at stake?
Voter ID. This would be a big change from how voting currently works in California.
Right now, election officials verify a voter’s identity when they register to vote. They also verify that the signature on a voter’s mail-in ballot matches the signature in their voter registration file.
But voters do not have to provide ID every time they cast a ballot.
Prop. 39 would change that and require voters to present a government-issued ID every time they vote.
The initiative would also shrink the long list of documents (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/regulations/hava_id_regs_from_barclays_3_3_06.pdf) the state currently accepts as proof of identity and residency for voting purposes. If Prop. 39 passes, only government-issued IDs, such as a driver’s license, passport, or state ID card, would be accepted.
The measure would require California to offer free state ID cards to eligible voters who lack another type of government-issued ID.
Official title on the ballot: Prop. 39: Prohibits citizens from voting unless they present government-issued identification
Language you will see: (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/index.htm)
Invalidates mail ballots that do not have last four digits of designated government-issued identification number written on envelope. Prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Fiscal Impact: Costs of between tens of millions of dollars and low hundreds of millions of dollars each year to implement new voting requirements.
What your vote means
A "yes" vote means: Voters would be required to present additional identifying information to elections officials each time they vote.
A "no" vote means: A voter’s identity would continue to be established with the voter’s signature.

Understanding Prop. 39
Currently, when someone registers to vote in California, they do not have to provide proof of citizenship. Rather, they have to check a box on their registration form attesting to being a U.S. citizen and California resident.
Lying on that form is a crime (perjury) punishable by fines and jail time.
Prop. 39 wouldn’t change that process.
What it would do is require election officials to make “best efforts” to verify the citizenship of people on voter registration rolls by cross-referencing their information against government data.
Why now?
According to a recent UC Berkeley poll (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/8hv8929c), just 22% of California Republicans surveyed have confidence in the election system, compared to 88% of Democrats. The two Republican legislators who proposed Prop. 39 see it as a step toward remedying that distrust.
President Donald Trump has also increasingly cast doubt on the integrity of elections across the U.S., including the claim that large numbers of noncitizens are voting. Efforts to find and prosecute noncitizen voters have thus far turned up few culprits (https://www.propublica.org/article/noncitizen-voting-trump-homeland-security-investigations).
But there have been a handful of recent cases in the news of noncitizens registering to vote, including a Honduran green card-holder who was charged with voter fraud (https://www.justice.gov/usao-cdca/pr/honduran-national-living-san-fernando-valley-arrested-federal-criminal-complaint) in August. Last year, an election integrity activist in Orange County was charged with fraud for registering and voting for her dog (https://laist.com/news/politics/dog-registered-to-vote-orange-county-redistricting-fight).
Here’s what supporters say
Supporters of Prop. 39 say requiring voter ID is a common sense reform to increase trust in the electoral process while maintaining voter conveniences including mail-in ballots. Supporters note that polling has found widespread support (https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2025/08/22/majority-of-americans-continue-to-back-expanded-early-voting-voting-by-mail-voter-id/) for voter ID across political parties. They also say using a voter’s signature on their mail-in ballot to verify identity, as California currently does, delays election results and causes some valid voters to have their ballots rejected.
Notable supporters: California Republican Party, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, Republican gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton, U.S. Congressman Ken Calvert (CA-41), Republican state Senator. Tony Strickland (Huntington Beach), Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (San Diego).
Here’s what opponents say
Opponents of Prop. 39 note that documented voter fraud is extremely rare (https://electionfraud.heritage.org/). They say the initiative feeds into Trump’s false claims of widespread election fraud, and would unfairly shut out eligible voters who make simple mistakes, like mixing up their ID number when writing it on their ballot envelope. They also say the federal government’s current system for verifying state voters’ eligibility is prone to error (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/watch-out-false-voter-fraud-claims-fueled-save-program).
Notable opposition: California Democratic Party, UCLA Voting Rights Project, U.S. Senator Alex Padilla, California Labor Federation
Potential financial impact
The state Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates that implementing Prop. 39 could cost anywhere from tens of millions to several hundred million dollars. Read the full analysis here (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=39&year=2026).

California Prop 39: What the voter ID measure may change & where it fits in the national battle
LAist's Jill Replogle shares what she’s learned from the author of Prop 39, its opponents and election experts.
This initiative would change California’s constitution to require voters to provide a government-issued ID when they cast a ballot. Mail-in voters would have to include the last four digits of their ID on the ballot envelope. The measure would also require election officials to use “best efforts,” using government data to verify that voters on registration rolls are U.S. citizens, and to report annually the percentage verified.
What’s at stake?
Voter ID. This would be a big change from how voting currently works in California.
Right now, election officials verify a voter’s identity when they register to vote. They also verify that the signature on a voter’s mail-in ballot matches the signature in their voter registration file.
But voters do not have to provide ID every time they cast a ballot.
Prop. 39 would change that and require voters to present a government-issued ID every time they vote.
The initiative would also shrink the long list of documents (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/regulations/hava_id_regs_from_barclays_3_3_06.pdf) the state currently accepts as proof of identity and residency for voting purposes. If Prop. 39 passes, only government-issued IDs, such as a driver’s license, passport, or state ID card, would be accepted.
The measure would require California to offer free state ID cards to eligible voters who lack another type of government-issued ID.
Official title on the ballot: Prop. 39: Prohibits citizens from voting unless they present government-issued identification
Language you will see: (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/index.htm)
Invalidates mail ballots that do not have last four digits of designated government-issued identification number written on envelope. Prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Fiscal Impact: Costs of between tens of millions of dollars and low hundreds of millions of dollars each year to implement new voting requirements.
What your vote means
A "yes" vote means: Voters would be required to present additional identifying information to elections officials each time they vote.
A "no" vote means: A voter’s identity would continue to be established with the voter’s signature.

Understanding Prop. 39
Currently, when someone registers to vote in California, they do not have to provide proof of citizenship. Rather, they have to check a box on their registration form attesting to being a U.S. citizen and California resident.
Lying on that form is a crime (perjury) punishable by fines and jail time.
Prop. 39 wouldn’t change that process.
What it would do is require election officials to make “best efforts” to verify the citizenship of people on voter registration rolls by cross-referencing their information against government data.
Why now?
According to a recent UC Berkeley poll (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/8hv8929c), just 22% of California Republicans surveyed have confidence in the election system, compared to 88% of Democrats. The two Republican legislators who proposed Prop. 39 see it as a step toward remedying that distrust.
President Donald Trump has also increasingly cast doubt on the integrity of elections across the U.S., including the claim that large numbers of noncitizens are voting. Efforts to find and prosecute noncitizen voters have thus far turned up few culprits (https://www.propublica.org/article/noncitizen-voting-trump-homeland-security-investigations).
But there have been a handful of recent cases in the news of noncitizens registering to vote, including a Honduran green card-holder who was charged with voter fraud (https://www.justice.gov/usao-cdca/pr/honduran-national-living-san-fernando-valley-arrested-federal-criminal-complaint) in August. Last year, an election integrity activist in Orange County was charged with fraud for registering and voting for her dog (https://laist.com/news/politics/dog-registered-to-vote-orange-county-redistricting-fight).
Here’s what supporters say
Supporters of Prop. 39 say requiring voter ID is a common sense reform to increase trust in the electoral process while maintaining voter conveniences including mail-in ballots. Supporters note that polling has found widespread support (https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2025/08/22/majority-of-americans-continue-to-back-expanded-early-voting-voting-by-mail-voter-id/) for voter ID across political parties. They also say using a voter’s signature on their mail-in ballot to verify identity, as California currently does, delays election results and causes some valid voters to have their ballots rejected.
Notable supporters: California Republican Party, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, Republican gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton, U.S. Congressman Ken Calvert (CA-41), Republican state Senator. Tony Strickland (Huntington Beach), Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (San Diego).
Here’s what opponents say
Opponents of Prop. 39 note that documented voter fraud is extremely rare (https://electionfraud.heritage.org/). They say the initiative feeds into Trump’s false claims of widespread election fraud, and would unfairly shut out eligible voters who make simple mistakes, like mixing up their ID number when writing it on their ballot envelope. They also say the federal government’s current system for verifying state voters’ eligibility is prone to error (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/watch-out-false-voter-fraud-claims-fueled-save-program).
Notable opposition: California Democratic Party, UCLA Voting Rights Project, U.S. Senator Alex Padilla, California Labor Federation
Potential financial impact
The state Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates that implementing Prop. 39 could cost anywhere from tens of millions to several hundred million dollars. Read the full analysis here (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=39&year=2026).

California Prop 39: What the voter ID measure may change & where it fits in the national battle
LAist's Jill Replogle shares what she’s learned from the author of Prop 39, its opponents and election experts.
This initiative would change California’s constitution to require voters to provide a government-issued ID when they cast a ballot. Mail-in voters would have to include the last four digits of their ID on the ballot envelope. The measure would also require election officials to use “best efforts,” using government data to verify that voters on registration rolls are U.S. citizens, and to report annually the percentage verified.
What’s at stake?
Voter ID. This would be a big change from how voting currently works in California.
Right now, election officials verify a voter’s identity when they register to vote. They also verify that the signature on a voter’s mail-in ballot matches the signature in their voter registration file.
But voters do not have to provide ID every time they cast a ballot.
Prop. 39 would change that and require voters to present a government-issued ID every time they vote.
The initiative would also shrink the long list of documents (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/regulations/hava_id_regs_from_barclays_3_3_06.pdf) the state currently accepts as proof of identity and residency for voting purposes. If Prop. 39 passes, only government-issued IDs, such as a driver’s license, passport, or state ID card, would be accepted.
The measure would require California to offer free state ID cards to eligible voters who lack another type of government-issued ID.
Official title on the ballot: Prop. 39: Prohibits citizens from voting unless they present government-issued identification
Language you will see: (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/index.htm)
Invalidates mail ballots that do not have last four digits of designated government-issued identification number written on envelope. Prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Fiscal Impact: Costs of between tens of millions of dollars and low hundreds of millions of dollars each year to implement new voting requirements.
What your vote means
A "yes" vote means: Voters would be required to present additional identifying information to elections officials each time they vote.
A "no" vote means: A voter’s identity would continue to be established with the voter’s signature.

Here's what voters need to know about the three seats up for election on the Pasadena Unified Board of Education.
Understanding Prop. 39
Currently, when someone registers to vote in California, they do not have to provide proof of citizenship. Rather, they have to check a box on their registration form attesting to being a U.S. citizen and California resident.
Lying on that form is a crime (perjury) punishable by fines and jail time.
Prop. 39 wouldn’t change that process.
What it would do is require election officials to make “best efforts” to verify the citizenship of people on voter registration rolls by cross-referencing their information against government data.
Why now?
According to a recent UC Berkeley poll (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/8hv8929c), just 22% of California Republicans surveyed have confidence in the election system, compared to 88% of Democrats. The two Republican legislators who proposed Prop. 39 see it as a step toward remedying that distrust.
President Donald Trump has also increasingly cast doubt on the integrity of elections across the U.S., including the claim that large numbers of noncitizens are voting. Efforts to find and prosecute noncitizen voters have thus far turned up few culprits (https://www.propublica.org/article/noncitizen-voting-trump-homeland-security-investigations).
But there have been a handful of recent cases in the news of noncitizens registering to vote, including a Honduran green card-holder who was charged with voter fraud (https://www.justice.gov/usao-cdca/pr/honduran-national-living-san-fernando-valley-arrested-federal-criminal-complaint) in August. Last year, an election integrity activist in Orange County was charged with fraud for registering and voting for her dog (https://laist.com/news/politics/dog-registered-to-vote-orange-county-redistricting-fight).
Here’s what supporters say
Supporters of Prop. 39 say requiring voter ID is a common sense reform to increase trust in the electoral process while maintaining voter conveniences including mail-in ballots. Supporters note that polling has found widespread support (https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2025/08/22/majority-of-americans-continue-to-back-expanded-early-voting-voting-by-mail-voter-id/) for voter ID across political parties. They also say using a voter’s signature on their mail-in ballot to verify identity, as California currently does, delays election results and causes some valid voters to have their ballots rejected.
Notable supporters: California Republican Party, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, Republican gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton, U.S. Congressman Ken Calvert (CA-41), Republican state Senator. Tony Strickland (Huntington Beach), Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (San Diego).
Here’s what opponents say
Opponents of Prop. 39 note that documented voter fraud is extremely rare (https://electionfraud.heritage.org/). They say the initiative feeds into Trump’s false claims of widespread election fraud, and would unfairly shut out eligible voters who make simple mistakes, like mixing up their ID number when writing it on their ballot envelope. They also say the federal government’s current system for verifying state voters’ eligibility is prone to error (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/watch-out-false-voter-fraud-claims-fueled-save-program).
Notable opposition: California Democratic Party, UCLA Voting Rights Project, U.S. Senator Alex Padilla, California Labor Federation
Potential financial impact
The state Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates that implementing Prop. 39 could cost anywhere from tens of millions to several hundred million dollars. Read the full analysis here (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=39&year=2026).

### Summary
Proposition 39 would establish new identification and citizenship-verification requirements for California elections.
State and local election officials would be required to make “best efforts,” using government records, to verify the U.S. citizenship of registered voters and report annually on the percentage verified in each county.
Voters would also have to select a government-issued form of identification when registering in order to vote by mail, and the state would provide a free voter identification card to anyone who requests one.
The measure would also require voters to provide identifying information each time they cast a ballot.
In-person voters would need to present government-issued identification, while mail voters would provide the last four digits of their selected identification number on the ballot envelope for verification.
Elections officials would confirm that the identification numbers provided on the ballot envelope match the voter’s registration information.The State Auditor would review state and county compliance every odd numbered year.
Proposition 39 mandates that the Legislature would need to clarify details not included in the proposition and they would have to pass additional laws before the measure could be fully implemented.

# Your guide to Proposition 39: Stricter voter ID requirements
Proposition 39 brings the national debate around U.S. election integrity home to California by proposing stricter new voter ID requirements for state elections — mandating that voters present government identification every time they vote in person, or cite a specific government ID number when voting by mail.

### What will the measure do?
Proposition 39 would require anyone voting in person in California to present a government-issued ID, and those voting by mail ballot to include the last four digits of the government-issued ID number they provided when they registered to vote.
In-person voters without ID would be turned away, while mail ballots without an attached ID number that matches their registration would be rejected.
Critics note the measure does not explicitly require election officials to reach out to voters to correct or “cure” a ballot that is missing an ID number before rejecting it, as they are required to do when a voter’s ballot signature does not match what’s on file.
The measure also would require the state to provide free voter ID cards to eligible voters upon request, and state and county election officials to verify the U.S. citizenship of registered voters using government data and publicly report the findings of that work.

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 39, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=39&year=2026), would require election officials to verify Californians’ U.S. citizenship and prohibit them from voting without a government-issued ID. It also creates other rules around the voting process and identity verification when voting in person vs. by mail and ongoing compliance checks.
Voting “yes” would mean that you need to present a government-issued ID to vote in person and if you’re voting by mail, you need to provide the last four digits of that ID.
Voting “no” means the process stays is it is — you don’t need to present an ID to vote and your citizenship is verified during the registration process.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Voter Identification, Citizenship Verification, and Registered Voter List Administration Initiative, see it as a common-sense solution to voter fraud and a way to boost confidence in our elections.
Opponents see it as an extension of the Republicans’ currently stalled SAVE America Act and Donald Trump’s unfounded assertion that he lost the 2020 election thanks to noncitizen voters. It is also seen as a way to reduce voter participation by making it harder to vote.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-39-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
How many illegal votes were cast in California’s last statewide election? I’m asking for a documented number, not an estimate of fraud you believe went undetected.
First, measuring fraud requires you to actually look for it and investigate it — neither of which is a priority of politicians right now in California. Second, whether you believe voter fraud is just a small problem or a big one, Prop. 39 is trying to solve a more serious and well-documented problem of public trust. A recent poll conducted by University of California, San Diego’s Center for Transparent and Trusted Elections showed 13% of Democratic voters have less confidence in elections than just two years ago — with 17% of Republicans and 16% of independent voters having less trust as well. Declining trust and confidence in elections is not a partisan problem — this is a democracy challenge that Prop. 39 fixes in a bipartisan way.

Of the documented cases, how many involved someone appearing at a polling place and impersonating another voter — the conduct that presenting ID in person would directly address?
First, your question incorrectly frames the problem Prop. 39 is trying to address — the dramatic decline in public trust in our elections. Polling consistently shows that a solid majority of Democratic, independent and Republican voters all say they would trust our elections more if we implemented Voter ID. Moreover, Prop. 39 will also ensure we improve identity verification for mail ballots by switching from the unreliable signature checks to the much easier four digits of a government ID.
Heritage describes its fraud database as a noncomprehensive “sampling” and makes no claim about the overall prevalence of fraud. Without comparing its selected cases with the billions of ballots cast, how can it establish that fraud is common enough to justify Prop. 39?
This question has now been answered twice above. You are missing the point of why Prop. 39 is needed — it is designed to improve public trust and confidence in our democracy. That is a big problem you seem to be ignoring here. With the polling showing declines in public trust — and support for reasonable voter ID requirements — why would you not want to implement Prop. 39 to improve trust and confidence in our elections?
California already establishes identity during registration and verifies mail-ballot signatures before counting them. What evidence shows these safeguards are failing often enough to require an additional check on every ballot?
First, Prop. 39 is about verifying identity when someone casts a ballot — not just when they register to vote. Second, a 2022 report by the Transparency Foundation showed an appalling lack of consistency in the signature checking process on mail-in ballots in many counties. Prop. 39 allows us to replace unreliable signature checks with an easier-to-use, four-digit PIN based on a government document of each voter’s choice.
The LAO estimates annual costs ranging from tens of millions to the low hundreds of millions of dollars. How many unlawful votes would Prop. 39 prevent each year, and what would taxpayers be paying per vote prevented?
The LAO cost estimate is wildly inaccurate and fails to account for the cost savings that would result by improving the accuracy of our voter rolls with saving on postage and printing of mail ballots. Prop. 39 will ultimately save money — while improving public trust and confidence in our democracy. Seems like a great return on investment.
The LAO says the measure could reduce registration among eligible voters who lack government-issued identification. How many eligible citizens is it acceptable to keep from voting to prevent one illegal vote?
This is absurd! Did requiring an ID to fly on an airplane reduce air traffic in the US? In states that have implemented voter ID, participation in voting has actually increased! Your question is grossly biased by falsely suggesting that citizens will be prevented from voting. Prop. 39 seeks to keep voting easy while improving identity checks in a balanced way to improve trust and confidence.
Prop. 39 requires “best efforts” to verify citizenship but does not define the term. Which government records are sufficiently complete and current to determine the citizenship of every registered voter?
First, it is not hard to define citizenship in the US — it is already well defined. Second, a variety of government databases exist to help election officials double check citizenship. That’s all Prop. 39 requires — which is why Prop. 39 is a balanced approach to implementing voter ID.
If government records cannot verify someone’s citizenship, does that person remain eligible to vote? If not, why should the government’s failure to find confirming information be treated as evidence that the person is ineligible?
Prop. 39 intentionally does not put any additional burdens on voters, which is why Prop. 39 specifically does not require that any voter provide documents to prove their citizenship to the government, as that is prohibited under current federal law. Instead Prop. 39 holds government officials accountable to double check citizenship using government databases.

How many eligible Californians do you expect Prop. 39 would prevent from voting, and what evidence supports that?
No one knows exactly how many eligible Californians Prop. 39 would block from voting, but we know that extra, unnecessary ID requirements don’t affect everyone equally. In other states, similar rules have led to eligible voters having their ballots rejected because of missing, incorrect or mismatched ID info. When Texas rolled out similar mail-ballot ID rules, mail ballot rejections shot up to 12% (https://www.texastribune.org/2022/04/06/texas-mail-in-ballot-rejection-voting/) and the Brennan Center for Justice found that Black, Latino and Asian voters had their ballots rejected at higher rates than white voters for ID mistakes or omissions. Recent studies, including from the University of Maryland (https://cdce.umd.edu/sites/cdce.umd.edu/files/pubs/Voter%20ID%20survey%20Key%20Results%20June%202024.pdf), have also shown that Californians are significantly less likely to have a current ID if they are people of color, younger, lower-income or have a disability. When eligible voters are turned away or their valid ballots are rejected, they’re less likely to try to participate in future elections.

The real question is whether adding another ID requirement would actually make our elections more secure, or just make it harder for people to vote. Evidence indicates that in-person impersonation is extremely rare. Does its rarity mean no additional precaution is warranted, even in an election decided by one or two votes?

The conservative Heritage Foundation found (https://www.businessinsider.com/voter-election-fraud-statistics-rare-president-biden-trump-2020-2020-11) that between 2000 and 2020, out of 250 million votes cast by mail in the U.S., there were only 193 proven fraud cases. The twin goals of elections should always be expanding access to increase participation for eligible citizens and ensuring the will of the voter though secure and accurate procedures. We have the second goal covered in California; we should focus more on the first one.

Every state, including California, has had rare and isolated cases of election misconduct, and those should be, and are, taken seriously. Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 39, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=39&year=2026), would require election officials to verify Californians’ U.S. citizenship and prohibit them from voting without a government-issued ID. It also creates other rules around the voting process and identity verification when voting in person vs. by mail and ongoing compliance checks.
Voting “yes” would mean that you need to present a government-issued ID to vote in person and if you’re voting by mail, you need to provide the last four digits of that ID.
Voting “no” means the process stays is it is — you don’t need to present an ID to vote and your citizenship is verified during the registration process.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Voter Identification, Citizenship Verification, and Registered Voter List Administration Initiative, see it as a common-sense solution to voter fraud and a way to boost confidence in our elections.
Opponents see it as an extension of the Republicans’ currently stalled SAVE America Act and Donald Trump’s unfounded assertion that he lost the 2020 election thanks to noncitizen voters. It is also seen as a way to reduce voter participation by making it harder to vote.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-39-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
How many illegal votes were cast in California’s last statewide election? I’m asking for a documented number, not an estimate of fraud you believe went undetected.
First, measuring fraud requires you to actually look for it and investigate it — neither of which is a priority of politicians right now in California. Second, whether you believe voter fraud is just a small problem or a big one, Prop. 39 is trying to solve a more serious and well-documented problem of public trust. A recent poll conducted by University of California, San Diego’s Center for Transparent and Trusted Elections showed 13% of Democratic voters have less confidence in elections than just two years ago — with 17% of Republicans and 16% of independent voters having less trust as well. Declining trust and confidence in elections is not a partisan problem — this is a democracy challenge that Prop. 39 fixes in a bipartisan way.

Of the documented cases, how many involved someone appearing at a polling place and impersonating another voter — the conduct that presenting ID in person would directly address?
First, your question incorrectly frames the problem Prop. 39 is trying to address — the dramatic decline in public trust in our elections. Polling consistently shows that a solid majority of Democratic, independent and Republican voters all say they would trust our elections more if we implemented Voter ID. Moreover, Prop. 39 will also ensure we improve identity verification for mail ballots by switching from the unreliable signature checks to the much easier four digits of a government ID.
Heritage describes its fraud database as a noncomprehensive “sampling” and makes no claim about the overall prevalence of fraud. Without comparing its selected cases with the billions of ballots cast, how can it establish that fraud is common enough to justify Prop. 39?
This question has now been answered twice above. You are missing the point of why Prop. 39 is needed — it is designed to improve public trust and confidence in our democracy. That is a big problem you seem to be ignoring here. With the polling showing declines in public trust — and support for reasonable voter ID requirements — why would you not want to implement Prop. 39 to improve trust and confidence in our elections?
California already establishes identity during registration and verifies mail-ballot signatures before counting them. What evidence shows these safeguards are failing often enough to require an additional check on every ballot?
First, Prop. 39 is about verifying identity when someone casts a ballot — not just when they register to vote. Second, a 2022 report by the Transparency Foundation showed an appalling lack of consistency in the signature checking process on mail-in ballots in many counties. Prop. 39 allows us to replace unreliable signature checks with an easier-to-use, four-digit PIN based on a government document of each voter’s choice.
The LAO estimates annual costs ranging from tens of millions to the low hundreds of millions of dollars. How many unlawful votes would Prop. 39 prevent each year, and what would taxpayers be paying per vote prevented?
The LAO cost estimate is wildly inaccurate and fails to account for the cost savings that would result by improving the accuracy of our voter rolls with saving on postage and printing of mail ballots. Prop. 39 will ultimately save money — while improving public trust and confidence in our democracy. Seems like a great return on investment.
The LAO says the measure could reduce registration among eligible voters who lack government-issued identification. How many eligible citizens is it acceptable to keep from voting to prevent one illegal vote?
This is absurd! Did requiring an ID to fly on an airplane reduce air traffic in the US? In states that have implemented voter ID, participation in voting has actually increased! Your question is grossly biased by falsely suggesting that citizens will be prevented from voting. Prop. 39 seeks to keep voting easy while improving identity checks in a balanced way to improve trust and confidence.
Prop. 39 requires “best efforts” to verify citizenship but does not define the term. Which government records are sufficiently complete and current to determine the citizenship of every registered voter?
First, it is not hard to define citizenship in the US — it is already well defined. Second, a variety of government databases exist to help election officials double check citizenship. That’s all Prop. 39 requires — which is why Prop. 39 is a balanced approach to implementing voter ID.
If government records cannot verify someone’s citizenship, does that person remain eligible to vote? If not, why should the government’s failure to find confirming information be treated as evidence that the person is ineligible?
Prop. 39 intentionally does not put any additional burdens on voters, which is why Prop. 39 specifically does not require that any voter provide documents to prove their citizenship to the government, as that is prohibited under current federal law. Instead Prop. 39 holds government officials accountable to double check citizenship using government databases.

By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.mercurynews.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: November 2, 2026 at 2:39 PM PST | UPDATED: November 2, 2026 at 6:04 PM PST

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 39, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=39&year=2026), would require election officials to verify Californians’ U.S. citizenship and prohibit them from voting without a government-issued ID. It also creates other rules around the voting process and identity verification when voting in person vs. by mail and ongoing compliance checks.
Voting “yes” would mean that you need to present a government-issued ID to vote in person and if you’re voting by mail, you need to provide the last four digits of that ID.
Voting “no” means the process stays is it is — you don’t need to present an ID to vote and your citizenship is verified during the registration process.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Voter Identification, Citizenship Verification, and Registered Voter List Administration Initiative, see it as a common-sense solution to voter fraud and a way to boost confidence in our elections.
Opponents see it as an extension of the Republicans’ currently stalled SAVE America Act and Donald Trump’s unfounded assertion that he lost the 2020 election thanks to noncitizen voters. It is also seen as a way to reduce voter participation by making it harder to vote.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-39-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
How many illegal votes were cast in California’s last statewide election? I’m asking for a documented number, not an estimate of fraud you believe went undetected.
First, measuring fraud requires you to actually look for it and investigate it — neither of which is a priority of politicians right now in California. Second, whether you believe voter fraud is just a small problem or a big one, Prop. 39 is trying to solve a more serious and well-documented problem of public trust. A recent poll conducted by University of California, San Diego’s Center for Transparent and Trusted Elections showed 13% of Democratic voters have less confidence in elections than just two years ago — with 17% of Republicans and 16% of independent voters having less trust as well. Declining trust and confidence in elections is not a partisan problem — this is a democracy challenge that Prop. 39 fixes in a bipartisan way.

Of the documented cases, how many involved someone appearing at a polling place and impersonating another voter — the conduct that presenting ID in person would directly address?
First, your question incorrectly frames the problem Prop. 39 is trying to address — the dramatic decline in public trust in our elections. Polling consistently shows that a solid majority of Democratic, independent and Republican voters all say they would trust our elections more if we implemented Voter ID. Moreover, Prop. 39 will also ensure we improve identity verification for mail ballots by switching from the unreliable signature checks to the much easier four digits of a government ID.
Heritage describes its fraud database as a noncomprehensive “sampling” and makes no claim about the overall prevalence of fraud. Without comparing its selected cases with the billions of ballots cast, how can it establish that fraud is common enough to justify Prop. 39?
This question has now been answered twice above. You are missing the point of why Prop. 39 is needed — it is designed to improve public trust and confidence in our democracy. That is a big problem you seem to be ignoring here. With the polling showing declines in public trust — and support for reasonable voter ID requirements — why would you not want to implement Prop. 39 to improve trust and confidence in our elections?
California already establishes identity during registration and verifies mail-ballot signatures before counting them. What evidence shows these safeguards are failing often enough to require an additional check on every ballot?
First, Prop. 39 is about verifying identity when someone casts a ballot — not just when they register to vote. Second, a 2022 report by the Transparency Foundation showed an appalling lack of consistency in the signature checking process on mail-in ballots in many counties. Prop. 39 allows us to replace unreliable signature checks with an easier-to-use, four-digit PIN based on a government document of each voter’s choice.
The LAO estimates annual costs ranging from tens of millions to the low hundreds of millions of dollars. How many unlawful votes would Prop. 39 prevent each year, and what would taxpayers be paying per vote prevented?
The LAO cost estimate is wildly inaccurate and fails to account for the cost savings that would result by improving the accuracy of our voter rolls with saving on postage and printing of mail ballots. Prop. 39 will ultimately save money — while improving public trust and confidence in our democracy. Seems like a great return on investment.
The LAO says the measure could reduce registration among eligible voters who lack government-issued identification. How many eligible citizens is it acceptable to keep from voting to prevent one illegal vote?
This is absurd! Did requiring an ID to fly on an airplane reduce air traffic in the US? In states that have implemented voter ID, participation in voting has actually increased! Your question is grossly biased by falsely suggesting that citizens will be prevented from voting. Prop. 39 seeks to keep voting easy while improving identity checks in a balanced way to improve trust and confidence.
Prop. 39 requires “best efforts” to verify citizenship but does not define the term. Which government records are sufficiently complete and current to determine the citizenship of every registered voter?
First, it is not hard to define citizenship in the US — it is already well defined. Second, a variety of government databases exist to help election officials double check citizenship. That’s all Prop. 39 requires — which is why Prop. 39 is a balanced approach to implementing voter ID.
If government records cannot verify someone’s citizenship, does that person remain eligible to vote? If not, why should the government’s failure to find confirming information be treated as evidence that the person is ineligible?
Prop. 39 intentionally does not put any additional burdens on voters, which is why Prop. 39 specifically does not require that any voter provide documents to prove their citizenship to the government, as that is prohibited under current federal law. Instead Prop. 39 holds government officials accountable to double check citizenship using government databases.
