Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 39, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=39&year=2026), would require election officials to verify Californians’ U.S. citizenship and prohibit them from voting without a government-issued ID. It also creates other rules around the voting process and identity verification when voting in person vs. by mail and ongoing compliance checks.
Voting “yes” would mean that you need to present a government-issued ID to vote in person and if you’re voting by mail, you need to provide the last four digits of that ID.
Voting “no” means the process stays is it is — you don’t need to present an ID to vote and your citizenship is verified during the registration process.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Voter Identification, Citizenship Verification, and Registered Voter List Administration Initiative, see it as a common-sense solution to voter fraud and a way to boost confidence in our elections.
Opponents see it as an extension of the Republicans’ currently stalled SAVE America Act and Donald Trump’s unfounded assertion that he lost the 2020 election thanks to noncitizen voters. It is also seen as a way to reduce voter participation by making it harder to vote.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the Yes campaign, go here (https://wp.me/p7ShJJ-SXLk).
How many eligible Californians do you expect Prop. 39 would prevent from voting, and what evidence supports that?
No one knows exactly how many eligible Californians Prop. 39 would block from voting, but we know that extra, unnecessary ID requirements don’t affect everyone equally. In other states, similar rules have led to eligible voters having their ballots rejected because of missing, incorrect or mismatched ID info. When Texas rolled out similar mail-ballot ID rules, mail ballot rejections shot up to 12% (https://www.texastribune.org/2022/04/06/texas-mail-in-ballot-rejection-voting/) and the Brennan Center for Justice found that Black, Latino and Asian voters had their ballots rejected at higher rates than white voters for ID mistakes or omissions. Recent studies, including from the University of Maryland (https://cdce.umd.edu/sites/cdce.umd.edu/files/pubs/Voter%20ID%20survey%20Key%20Results%20June%202024.pdf), have also shown that Californians are significantly less likely to have a current ID if they are people of color, younger, lower-income or have a disability. When eligible voters are turned away or their valid ballots are rejected, they’re less likely to try to participate in future elections.

The state would provide a voter ID card at no cost to voters who request one. What barriers would remain for eligible voters?
Even if the voter ID card is free, plenty of hurdles remain. People still have to take time off work, arrange transportation and childcare, gather paperwork or pay fees to get copies of documents like birth certificates and deal with bureaucracy. For anyone with mobility issues, a tight schedule, limited financial resources or trouble accessing government offices, these steps can go from inconveniences, to challenges, and then become real barriers — and all to satisfy disproven election conspiracies. In short, just because something is free doesn’t mean it’s easy or accessible for everyone. Requiring the state to issue IDs just for voting, when our elections are already secure, pushes underrepresented voters further out of democracy and wastes a massive amount of taxpayer money.
In-person voters currently identify themselves by signing the voter roster, but the LAO says those signatures generally are not verified before ballots are counted. Is that adequate?
California already has a safe and accessible process to check that someone is registered and eligible to vote at the polls. Election officials verify the identity and eligibility of everyone in the voter registration database and regularly maintain and update those records using reliable sources, including DMV and Social Security records. Requiring in-person voters who have already been verified to provide name, address and a signature swearing under penalty of law that they are who they say they are ensures security without creating new barriers. The real question is whether adding another ID requirement would actually make our elections more secure, or just make it harder for people to vote. Prop. 39 offers no evidence that it makes elections safer, and a court held (https://www.courthousenews.com/california-judge-rules-voter-id-supporters-must-rewrite-ballot-arguments/) that imposing this “extra step” on voters certainly doesn’t make voting easier.
Evidence indicates that in-person impersonation is extremely rare. Does its rarity mean no additional precaution is warranted, even in an election decided by one or two votes?
We should only add new rules if they address an actual problem and the benefits outweigh the downsides for eligible voters. The conservative Heritage Foundation found (https://www.businessinsider.com/voter-election-fraud-statistics-rare-president-biden-trump-2020-2020-11) that between 2000 and 2020, out of 250 million votes cast by mail in the U.S., there were only 193 proven fraud cases. The Brennan Center also found that in-person voter impersonation is so rare that someone is more likely to be struck by lightning. These numbers show that our elections are already secure. Prop. 39 isn’t a precaution — it’s unnecessary and adds expensive bureaucratic barriers that could block millions of eligible Californians from voting. The twin goals of elections should always be expanding access to increase participation for eligible citizens and ensuring the will of the voter though secure and accurate procedures. We have the second goal covered in California; we should focus more on the first one.
Heritage’s database does not establish a fraud rate, but it documents proven election offenses. Which documented vulnerabilities do you believe California’s current system has not adequately addressed?
Every state, including California, has had rare and isolated cases of election misconduct, and those should be, and are, taken seriously. But a handful of cases — out of hundreds of millions of votes — doesn’t mean there’s a big flaw in the system. It means the system is working effectively to keep the number so dramatically low. California already has strong, well-researched and tested processes to keep voter rolls up to date, check registration information, prevent double voting or impersonation and audit ballots. PUBLISHED: November 2, 2026 at 2:52 PM PST | UPDATED: November 2, 2026 at 6:04 PM PST
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 39, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=39&year=2026), would require election officials to verify Californians’ U.S. citizenship and prohibit them from voting without a government-issued ID. It also creates other rules around the voting process and identity verification when voting in person vs. by mail and ongoing compliance checks.
Voting “yes” would mean that you need to present a government-issued ID to vote in person and if you’re voting by mail, you need to provide the last four digits of that ID.
Voting “no” means the process stays is it is — you don’t need to present an ID to vote and your citizenship is verified during the registration process.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Voter Identification, Citizenship Verification, and Registered Voter List Administration Initiative, see it as a common-sense solution to voter fraud and a way to boost confidence in our elections.
Opponents see it as an extension of the Republicans’ currently stalled SAVE America Act and Donald Trump’s unfounded assertion that he lost the 2020 election thanks to noncitizen voters. It is also seen as a way to reduce voter participation by making it harder to vote.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the Yes campaign, go here (https://wp.me/p7ShJJ-SXLk).
How many eligible Californians do you expect Prop. 39 would prevent from voting, and what evidence supports that?
No one knows exactly how many eligible Californians Prop. 39 would block from voting, but we know that extra, unnecessary ID requirements don’t affect everyone equally. In other states, similar rules have led to eligible voters having their ballots rejected because of missing, incorrect or mismatched ID info. When Texas rolled out similar mail-ballot ID rules, mail ballot rejections shot up to 12% (https://www.texastribune.org/2022/04/06/texas-mail-in-ballot-rejection-voting/) and the Brennan Center for Justice found that Black, Latino and Asian voters had their ballots rejected at higher rates than white voters for ID mistakes or omissions. Recent studies, including from the University of Maryland (https://cdce.umd.edu/sites/cdce.umd.edu/files/pubs/Voter%20ID%20survey%20Key%20Results%20June%202024.pdf), have also shown that Californians are significantly less likely to have a current ID if they are people of color, younger, lower-income or have a disability. When eligible voters are turned away or their valid ballots are rejected, they’re less likely to try to participate in future elections.
Related Articles
We asked the No on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the No on Prop. 41 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 41 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 5 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
The state would provide a voter ID card at no cost to voters who request one. What barriers would remain for eligible voters?
Even if the voter ID card is free, plenty of hurdles remain. People still have to take time off work, arrange transportation and childcare, gather paperwork or pay fees to get copies of documents like birth certificates and deal with bureaucracy. For anyone with mobility issues, a tight schedule, limited financial resources or trouble accessing government offices, these steps can go from inconveniences, to challenges, and then become real barriers — and all to satisfy disproven election conspiracies. In short, just because something is free doesn’t mean it’s easy or accessible for everyone. Requiring the state to issue IDs just for voting, when our elections are already secure, pushes underrepresented voters further out of democracy and wastes a massive amount of taxpayer money.
In-person voters currently identify themselves by signing the voter roster, but the LAO says those signatures generally are not verified before ballots are counted. Is that adequate?
California already has a safe and accessible process to check that someone is registered and eligible to vote at the polls. Election officials verify the identity and eligibility of everyone in the voter registration database and regularly maintain and update those records using reliable sources, including DMV and Social Security records. Requiring in-person voters who have already been verified to provide name, address and a signature swearing under penalty of law that they are who they say they are ensures security without creating new barriers. The real question is whether adding another ID requirement would actually make our elections more secure, or just make it harder for people to vote. Prop. 39 offers no evidence that it makes elections safer, and a court held (https://www.courthousenews.com/california-judge-rules-voter-id-supporters-must-rewrite-ballot-arguments/) that imposing this “extra step” on voters certainly doesn’t make voting easier.
Evidence indicates that in-person impersonation is extremely rare. Does its rarity mean no additional precaution is warranted, even in an election decided by one or two votes?
We should only add new rules if they address an actual problem and the benefits outweigh the downsides for eligible voters. The conservative Heritage Foundation found (https://www.businessinsider.com/voter-election-fraud-statistics-rare-president-biden-trump-2020-2020-11) that between 2000 and 2020, out of 250 million votes cast by mail in the U.S., there were only 193 proven fraud cases. The Brennan Center also found that in-person voter impersonation is so rare that someone is more likely to be struck by lightning. These numbers show that our elections are already secure. Prop. 39 isn’t a precaution — it’s unnecessary and adds expensive bureaucratic barriers that could block millions of eligible Californians from voting. The twin goals of elections should always be expanding access to increase participation for eligible citizens and ensuring the will of the voter though secure and accurate procedures. We have the second goal covered in California; we should focus more on the first one.
Heritage’s database does not establish a fraud rate, but it documents proven election offenses. Which documented vulnerabilities do you believe California’s current system has not adequately addressed?
Every state, including California, has had rare and isolated cases of election misconduct, and those should be, and are, taken seriously. But a handful of cases — out of hundreds of millions of votes — doesn’t mean there’s a big flaw in the system. It means the system is working effectively to keep the number so dramatically low. California already has strong, well-researched and tested processes to keep voter rolls up to date, check registration information, prevent double voting or impersonation and audit ballots. First, measuring fraud requires you to actually look for it and investigate it — neither of which is a priority of politicians right now in California. Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 39, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=39&year=2026), would require election officials to verify Californians’ U.S. citizenship and prohibit them from voting without a government-issued ID. It also creates other rules around the voting process and identity verification when voting in person vs. by mail and ongoing compliance checks.
Voting “yes” would mean that you need to present a government-issued ID to vote in person and if you’re voting by mail, you need to provide the last four digits of that ID.
Voting “no” means the process stays is it is — you don’t need to present an ID to vote and your citizenship is verified during the registration process.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Voter Identification, Citizenship Verification, and Registered Voter List Administration Initiative, see it as a common-sense solution to voter fraud and a way to boost confidence in our elections.
Opponents see it as an extension of the Republicans’ currently stalled SAVE America Act and Donald Trump’s unfounded assertion that he lost the 2020 election thanks to noncitizen voters. It is also seen as a way to reduce voter participation by making it harder to vote.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the Yes campaign, go here (https://wp.me/p7ShJJ-SXLk).
How many eligible Californians do you expect Prop. 39 would prevent from voting, and what evidence supports that?
No one knows exactly how many eligible Californians Prop. 39 would block from voting, but we know that extra, unnecessary ID requirements don’t affect everyone equally. In other states, similar rules have led to eligible voters having their ballots rejected because of missing, incorrect or mismatched ID info. When Texas rolled out similar mail-ballot ID rules, mail ballot rejections shot up to 12% (https://www.texastribune.org/2022/04/06/texas-mail-in-ballot-rejection-voting/) and the Brennan Center for Justice found that Black, Latino and Asian voters had their ballots rejected at higher rates than white voters for ID mistakes or omissions. Recent studies, including from the University of Maryland (https://cdce.umd.edu/sites/cdce.umd.edu/files/pubs/Voter%20ID%20survey%20Key%20Results%20June%202024.pdf), have also shown that Californians are significantly less likely to have a current ID if they are people of color, younger, lower-income or have a disability. When eligible voters are turned away or their valid ballots are rejected, they’re less likely to try to participate in future elections.

The state would provide a voter ID card at no cost to voters who request one. What barriers would remain for eligible voters?
Even if the voter ID card is free, plenty of hurdles remain. People still have to take time off work, arrange transportation and childcare, gather paperwork or pay fees to get copies of documents like birth certificates and deal with bureaucracy. For anyone with mobility issues, a tight schedule, limited financial resources or trouble accessing government offices, these steps can go from inconveniences, to challenges, and then become real barriers — and all to satisfy disproven election conspiracies. In short, just because something is free doesn’t mean it’s easy or accessible for everyone. Requiring the state to issue IDs just for voting, when our elections are already secure, pushes underrepresented voters further out of democracy and wastes a massive amount of taxpayer money.
In-person voters currently identify themselves by signing the voter roster, but the LAO says those signatures generally are not verified before ballots are counted. Is that adequate?
California already has a safe and accessible process to check that someone is registered and eligible to vote at the polls. Election officials verify the identity and eligibility of everyone in the voter registration database and regularly maintain and update those records using reliable sources, including DMV and Social Security records. Requiring in-person voters who have already been verified to provide name, address and a signature swearing under penalty of law that they are who they say they are ensures security without creating new barriers. The real question is whether adding another ID requirement would actually make our elections more secure, or just make it harder for people to vote. Prop. 39 offers no evidence that it makes elections safer, and a court held (https://www.courthousenews.com/california-judge-rules-voter-id-supporters-must-rewrite-ballot-arguments/) that imposing this “extra step” on voters certainly doesn’t make voting easier.
Evidence indicates that in-person impersonation is extremely rare. Does its rarity mean no additional precaution is warranted, even in an election decided by one or two votes?
We should only add new rules if they address an actual problem and the benefits outweigh the downsides for eligible voters. The conservative Heritage Foundation found (https://www.businessinsider.com/voter-election-fraud-statistics-rare-president-biden-trump-2020-2020-11) that between 2000 and 2020, out of 250 million votes cast by mail in the U.S., there were only 193 proven fraud cases. The Brennan Center also found that in-person voter impersonation is so rare that someone is more likely to be struck by lightning. These numbers show that our elections are already secure. Prop. 39 fixes a serious problem with the current mail-ballot verification process, which relies solely on signature matches — and some voters’ signatures have changed over the years and their ballots are being invalidated as a result. In the last election more than 100,000 mail ballots were rejected due to signature mismatches. Prop. 39 replaces that process with four digits from a government ID to ensure every eligible vote is counted — and allows a “curring” process if a voter transposes numbers to make sure every valid vote counts.
The proposition leaves the Legislature to decide which identifications qualify and what constitutes “best efforts” citizenship verification. Why should Californians amend their Constitution before knowing the rules that will determine whether their ballots are counted?
No, that is not true. Prop. 39’s reference to “best efforts” simply establishes the expectation that our county election offices do their best job in maintaining their voter rolls. The Legislature can help clarify that, but ultimately, Prop. 39 gives courts the authority to ensure proper compliance with the expectations voters are imposing to improve election management. California is currently not using widely accepted list management practices that are used in red and blue states across the country.
What elections in California over the last 100 years should be called into question because the number of illegal votes was officially found to be high enough to have swung the results?
This question is not relevant to the stated goal of Prop. 39 — which is to improve public trust and confidence in our democracy going forward. We are not engaging in conspiracy theories or accusations about stolen elections because that is exactly counter to our goal of restoring trust through widely supported bipartisan election integrity reforms.
What do opponents of Prop. 39 get most wrong?
Opponents of Prop. 39 falsely claim this is a Donald Trump scheme. Prop. 39 is absolutely not the same as Trump’s SAVE Act. Prop. 39 is the bipartisan alternative to implementing voter ID in a balanced way without burdens on voters — and with the singular goal of improving trust and confidence in our elections. We believe Prop. 39 will become the national model for how to get voter ID done in a bipartisan way, and California citizens need to lead the way where partisan politicians have failed us.

backed by evidence that current safeguards aren’t enough. Otherwise, it only creates new barriers for eligible voters, which compounds the real problem of low and unequal turnout by eligible voters in our democracy.
California currently verifies mail-ballot signatures. What is your objection to adding a match of four identification digits, assuming eligible voters receive notice and an opportunity to correct mistakes?
The problem is that Prop. 39 layers unnecessary stumbling blocks onto a process that’s already working, creating more ways for a legitimate mail ballot to get tossed out. California already checks signatures on mail ballots and gives people a chance to fix signature issues, and that’s in addition to the registration verification and ballot tracking the state does. Prop. 39 would require mail voters to “designate” a specific ID number to use for voting, remember potentially years later which form of ID they designated, and perfectly match the last digits of that number each time they vote. This means another hoop to jump through, and voters can easily get tripped up if they write the wrong digits or provide a signature but not the ID number. And Prop. 39 doesn’t provide a way for voters to fix these simple mistakes — or even receive notice — before their ballot is thrown out.
Citizenship is already required for federal, state and almost all California local elections. What is objectionable about asking officials to use government data to make “best efforts” to verify that registered voters are citizens?
Citizenship is already a voting requirement in the California Constitution. Anyone registering to vote must swear, under penalty of perjury, that they’re a U.S. citizen. California keeps a statewide registration system and regularly checks the rolls against reliable databases. Prop. 39 is adding another layer of “citizenship checks” that would mistakenly flag some naturalized citizens as noncitizens, especially since no comprehensive government database of U.S. citizenship exists. Recent ProPublica reporting on similar checks using Trump’s SAVE database revealed that this could yield an “ungodly” number of false positives (https://www.propublica.org/article/noncitizen-voting-trump-homeland-security-investigations). Prop. 39 would force a vague mandate on election workers who are already overworked and they’d have to repeat this wasteful and error-prone task annually. Before we add yet another verification layer, subject to mistake or political abuse, we need strong evidence that the current system isn’t working and that the new process won’t block eligible voters.
Prop. 39 does not specify that a voter must be removed merely because citizenship cannot be verified through government data. Are opponents distinguishing between what the measure expressly requires and what future implementing legislation might require?
Prop. 39 doesn’t mandate removing a voter just because their citizenship couldn’t be confirmed — but the concern is implementation. Experts agree that there is no complete, accurate list of who is and isn’t a U.S. citizen, which means any fishing expedition conducted because of Prop. 39 would result in error-filled reports. This fuels confusion, disinformation and mistrust in our elections, giving ammunition to bad actors who want eligible voters purged from the rolls. Prop. 39 also lets private actors sue elections officials, forcing underresourced local governments to choose between caving to demands for overly aggressive voter purges and spending taxpayer money to defend against frivolous litigation. Because so many details are left open, future changes or court cases could create new problems for voters flagged by the process. So, it’s not just about what’s written in Prop. 39; it’s also about the uncertainty it creates down the line.
The measure requires annual reporting of the percentage of registered voters whose citizenship has been verified and biennial state auditor reviews of state and county compliance. Do you oppose those requirements themselves, or primarily their cost and connection to the identification mandate?
We’re concerned about both. California already requires voters to swear they’re citizens and has proven systems to check registration information and keep the rolls up to date. Prop. 39 would add redundant, wasteful and potentially dangerous mandates to the work of our trusted and under-resourced elections officials without showing that the current system is broken. It would also require ongoing reporting and audits, which could cost state and local governments tens or even hundreds of millions of dollars each year, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office. We should be asking whether these costs actually solve a real problem before making taxpayers and county election officials pay the price.
If your objection is that Prop. 39 leaves critical protections to future legislation, would you support a narrower law that specifies broadly acceptable ID, provisional voting, advance notice and a guaranteed opportunity to correct errors? If not, is your objection to this measure’s drafting or to voter ID requirements generally?
The main issue is that Prop. 39’s new requirements would create unnecessary new hurdles for eligible voters and new ways to reject valid ballots, without offering any evidence that there’s a problem it would solve. Voter participation rates in the U.S. are already amongst the lowest for many industrialized countries. We also have concerns about how Prop. 39 is written since it leaves many important details to future laws, like which IDs would be accepted, whether mail voters would get notice or a chance to fix mistakes with their ID number, and what counts as “best efforts” for citizenship checks. The Legislative Analyst’s Office provided a large cost-estimate range because so much is left undefined in Prop. 39. Election laws should keep voting secure without making it harder for people who have the right to vote.
What do proponents of this get most wrong?
Proponents get two big things wrong. First, California’s elections are already safe and secure, with strong systems for checking voter registration and keeping the rolls accurate and up to date. Second, Prop. 39 would fundamentally change how we vote; more than 80% of Californians voted by mail in the 2024 presidential election. Prop. 39 would force those voters to add the last four digits of a specific ID number to their ballot envelope, creating the risk of ballot rejection for simple errors and exposing them to identity theft. It would add new ID requirements for in-person voters and subject all voters to repeated, faulty citizenship checks. This isn’t just a small administrative tweak; it’s a major change, backed by MAGA billionaires (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316461529.html) and demanded by President Trump, who called for it as a precondition for California receiving federal aid after the 2025 Southern California wildfires. That context matters here.

California currently verifies mail-ballot signatures. What is your objection to adding a match of four identification digits, assuming eligible voters receive notice and an opportunity to correct mistakes?
The problem is that Prop. 39 layers unnecessary stumbling blocks onto a process that’s already working, creating more ways for a legitimate mail ballot to get tossed out. California already checks signatures on mail ballots and gives people a chance to fix signature issues, and that’s in addition to the registration verification and ballot tracking the state does. Prop. 39 would require mail voters to “designate” a specific ID number to use for voting, remember potentially years later which form of ID they designated, and perfectly match the last digits of that number each time they vote. This means another hoop to jump through, and voters can easily get tripped up if they write the wrong digits or provide a signature but not the ID number. And Prop. 39 doesn’t provide a way for voters to fix these simple mistakes — or even receive notice — before their ballot is thrown out.
Citizenship is already required for federal, state and almost all California local elections. What is objectionable about asking officials to use government data to make “best efforts” to verify that registered voters are citizens?
Citizenship is already a voting requirement in the California Constitution. Anyone registering to vote must swear, under penalty of perjury, that they’re a U.S. citizen. California keeps a statewide registration system and regularly checks the rolls against reliable databases. Prop. 39 is adding another layer of “citizenship checks” that would mistakenly flag some naturalized citizens as noncitizens, especially since no comprehensive government database of U.S. citizenship exists. Recent ProPublica reporting on similar checks using Trump’s SAVE database revealed that this could yield an “ungodly” number of false positives (https://www.propublica.org/article/noncitizen-voting-trump-homeland-security-investigations). Prop. 39 would force a vague mandate on election workers who are already overworked and they’d have to repeat this wasteful and error-prone task annually. Before we add yet another verification layer, subject to mistake or political abuse, we need strong evidence that the current system isn’t working and that the new process won’t block eligible voters.
Prop. 39 does not specify that a voter must be removed merely because citizenship cannot be verified through government data. Are opponents distinguishing between what the measure expressly requires and what future implementing legislation might require?
Prop. 39 doesn’t mandate removing a voter just because their citizenship couldn’t be confirmed — but the concern is implementation. Experts agree that there is no complete, accurate list of who is and isn’t a U.S. citizen, which means any fishing expedition conducted because of Prop. 39 would result in error-filled reports. This fuels confusion, disinformation and mistrust in our elections, giving ammunition to bad actors who want eligible voters purged from the rolls. Prop. 39 also lets private actors sue elections officials, forcing underresourced local governments to choose between caving to demands for overly aggressive voter purges and spending taxpayer money to defend against frivolous litigation. Because so many details are left open, future changes or court cases could create new problems for voters flagged by the process. So, it’s not just about what’s written in Prop. 39; it’s also about the uncertainty it creates down the line.
The measure requires annual reporting of the percentage of registered voters whose citizenship has been verified and biennial state auditor reviews of state and county compliance. Do you oppose those requirements themselves, or primarily their cost and connection to the identification mandate?
We’re concerned about both. California already requires voters to swear they’re citizens and has proven systems to check registration information and keep the rolls up to date. Prop. 39 would add redundant, wasteful and potentially dangerous mandates to the work of our trusted and under-resourced elections officials without showing that the current system is broken. It would also require ongoing reporting and audits, which could cost state and local governments tens or even hundreds of millions of dollars each year, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office. We should be asking whether these costs actually solve a real problem before making taxpayers and county election officials pay the price.
If your objection is that Prop. 39 leaves critical protections to future legislation, would you support a narrower law that specifies broadly acceptable ID, provisional voting, advance notice and a guaranteed opportunity to correct errors? If not, is your objection to this measure’s drafting or to voter ID requirements generally?
The main issue is that Prop. 39’s new requirements would create unnecessary new hurdles for eligible voters and new ways to reject valid ballots, without offering any evidence that there’s a problem it would solve. Voter participation rates in the U.S. are already amongst the lowest for many industrialized countries. We also have concerns about how Prop. 39 is written since it leaves many important details to future laws, like which IDs would be accepted, whether mail voters would get notice or a chance to fix mistakes with their ID number, and what counts as “best efforts” for citizenship checks. The Legislative Analyst’s Office provided a large cost-estimate range because so much is left undefined in Prop. 39. Election laws should keep voting secure without making it harder for people who have the right to vote.
What do proponents of this get most wrong?
Proponents get two big things wrong. First, California’s elections are already safe and secure, with strong systems for checking voter registration and keeping the rolls accurate and up to date. Second, Prop. 39 would fundamentally change how we vote; more than 80% of Californians voted by mail in the 2024 presidential election. Prop. 39 would force those voters to add the last four digits of a specific ID number to their ballot envelope, creating the risk of ballot rejection for simple errors and exposing them to identity theft. It would add new ID requirements for in-person voters and subject all voters to repeated, faulty citizenship checks. This isn’t just a small administrative tweak; it’s a major change, backed by MAGA billionaires (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316461529.html) and demanded by President Trump, who called for it as a precondition for California receiving federal aid after the 2025 Southern California wildfires. That context matters here.

backed by evidence that current safeguards aren’t enough. Otherwise, it only creates new barriers for eligible voters, which compounds the real problem of low and unequal turnout by eligible voters in our democracy.
California currently verifies mail-ballot signatures. What is your objection to adding a match of four identification digits, assuming eligible voters receive notice and an opportunity to correct mistakes?
The problem is that Prop. 39 layers unnecessary stumbling blocks onto a process that’s already working, creating more ways for a legitimate mail ballot to get tossed out. California already checks signatures on mail ballots and gives people a chance to fix signature issues, and that’s in addition to the registration verification and ballot tracking the state does. Prop. 39 would require mail voters to “designate” a specific ID number to use for voting, remember potentially years later which form of ID they designated, and perfectly match the last digits of that number each time they vote. This means another hoop to jump through, and voters can easily get tripped up if they write the wrong digits or provide a signature but not the ID number. And Prop. 39 doesn’t provide a way for voters to fix these simple mistakes — or even receive notice — before their ballot is thrown out.
Citizenship is already required for federal, state and almost all California local elections. What is objectionable about asking officials to use government data to make “best efforts” to verify that registered voters are citizens?
Citizenship is already a voting requirement in the California Constitution. Anyone registering to vote must swear, under penalty of perjury, that they’re a U.S. citizen. California keeps a statewide registration system and regularly checks the rolls against reliable databases. Prop. 39 is adding another layer of “citizenship checks” that would mistakenly flag some naturalized citizens as noncitizens, especially since no comprehensive government database of U.S. citizenship exists. Recent ProPublica reporting on similar checks using Trump’s SAVE database revealed that this could yield an “ungodly” number of false positives (https://www.propublica.org/article/noncitizen-voting-trump-homeland-security-investigations). Prop. 39 would force a vague mandate on election workers who are already overworked and they’d have to repeat this wasteful and error-prone task annually. Before we add yet another verification layer, subject to mistake or political abuse, we need strong evidence that the current system isn’t working and that the new process won’t block eligible voters.
Prop. 39 does not specify that a voter must be removed merely because citizenship cannot be verified through government data. Are opponents distinguishing between what the measure expressly requires and what future implementing legislation might require?
Prop. 39 doesn’t mandate removing a voter just because their citizenship couldn’t be confirmed — but the concern is implementation. Experts agree that there is no complete, accurate list of who is and isn’t a U.S. citizen, which means any fishing expedition conducted because of Prop. 39 would result in error-filled reports. This fuels confusion, disinformation and mistrust in our elections, giving ammunition to bad actors who want eligible voters purged from the rolls. Prop. 39 also lets private actors sue elections officials, forcing underresourced local governments to choose between caving to demands for overly aggressive voter purges and spending taxpayer money to defend against frivolous litigation. Because so many details are left open, future changes or court cases could create new problems for voters flagged by the process. So, it’s not just about what’s written in Prop. 39; it’s also about the uncertainty it creates down the line.
The measure requires annual reporting of the percentage of registered voters whose citizenship has been verified and biennial state auditor reviews of state and county compliance. Do you oppose those requirements themselves, or primarily their cost and connection to the identification mandate?
We’re concerned about both. California already requires voters to swear they’re citizens and has proven systems to check registration information and keep the rolls up to date. Prop. 39 would add redundant, wasteful and potentially dangerous mandates to the work of our trusted and under-resourced elections officials without showing that the current system is broken. It would also require ongoing reporting and audits, which could cost state and local governments tens or even hundreds of millions of dollars each year, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office. We should be asking whether these costs actually solve a real problem before making taxpayers and county election officials pay the price.
If your objection is that Prop. 39 leaves critical protections to future legislation, would you support a narrower law that specifies broadly acceptable ID, provisional voting, advance notice and a guaranteed opportunity to correct errors? If not, is your objection to this measure’s drafting or to voter ID requirements generally?
The main issue is that Prop. 39’s new requirements would create unnecessary new hurdles for eligible voters and new ways to reject valid ballots, without offering any evidence that there’s a problem it would solve. Voter participation rates in the U.S. are already amongst the lowest for many industrialized countries. We also have concerns about how Prop. 39 is written since it leaves many important details to future laws, like which IDs would be accepted, whether mail voters would get notice or a chance to fix mistakes with their ID number, and what counts as “best efforts” for citizenship checks. The Legislative Analyst’s Office provided a large cost-estimate range because so much is left undefined in Prop. 39. Election laws should keep voting secure without making it harder for people who have the right to vote.
What do proponents of this get most wrong?
Proponents get two big things wrong. First, California’s elections are already safe and secure, with strong systems for checking voter registration and keeping the rolls accurate and up to date. Second, Prop. 39 would fundamentally change how we vote; more than 80% of Californians voted by mail in the 2024 presidential election. Prop. 39 would force those voters to add the last four digits of a specific ID number to their ballot envelope, creating the risk of ballot rejection for simple errors and exposing them to identity theft. It would add new ID requirements for in-person voters and subject all voters to repeated, faulty citizenship checks. This isn’t just a small administrative tweak; it’s a major change, backed by MAGA billionaires (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316461529.html) and demanded by President Trump, who called for it as a precondition for California receiving federal aid after the 2025 Southern California wildfires. That context matters here.

content.text:
last four digits of the government ID selected in the voter’s registration. What happens if an eligible voter transposes two digits, omits them, renews the ID or provides digits from a different valid ID?
Prop. 39 fixes a serious problem with the current mail-ballot verification process, which relies solely on signature matches — and some voters’ signatures have changed over the years and their ballots are being invalidated as a result. In the last election more than 100,000 mail ballots were rejected due to signature mismatches. Prop. 39 replaces that process with four digits from a government ID to ensure every eligible vote is counted — and allows a “curring” process if a voter transposes numbers to make sure every valid vote counts.
The proposition leaves the Legislature to decide which identifications qualify and what constitutes “best efforts” citizenship verification. Why should Californians amend their Constitution before knowing the rules that will determine whether their ballots are counted?
No, that is not true. Prop. 39’s reference to “best efforts” simply establishes the expectation that our county election offices do their best job in maintaining their voter rolls. The Legislature can help clarify that, but ultimately, Prop. 39 gives courts the authority to ensure proper compliance with the expectations voters are imposing to improve election management. California is currently not using widely accepted list management practices that are used in red and blue states across the country.
What elections in California over the last 100 years should be called into question because the number of illegal votes was officially found to be high enough to have swung the results?
This question is not relevant to the stated goal of Prop. 39 — which is to improve public trust and confidence in our democracy going forward. We are not engaging in conspiracy theories or accusations about stolen elections because that is exactly counter to our goal of restoring trust through widely supported bipartisan election integrity reforms.
What do opponents of Prop. 39 get most wrong?
Opponents of Prop. 39 falsely claim this is a Donald Trump scheme. Prop. 39 is absolutely not the same as Trump’s SAVE Act. Prop. 39 is the bipartisan alternative to implementing voter ID in a balanced way without burdens on voters — and with the singular goal of improving trust and confidence in our elections. We believe Prop. 39 will become the national model for how to get voter ID done in a bipartisan way, and California citizens need to lead the way where partisan politicians have failed us.

backed by evidence that current safeguards aren’t enough. Otherwise, it only creates new barriers for eligible voters, which compounds the real problem of low and unequal turnout by eligible voters in our democracy.
California currently verifies mail-ballot signatures. What is your objection to adding a match of four identification digits, assuming eligible voters receive notice and an opportunity to correct mistakes?
The problem is that Prop. 39 layers unnecessary stumbling blocks onto a process that’s already working, creating more ways for a legitimate mail ballot to get tossed out. California already checks signatures on mail ballots and gives people a chance to fix signature issues, and that’s in addition to the registration verification and ballot tracking the state does. Prop. 39 would require mail voters to “designate” a specific ID number to use for voting, remember potentially years later which form of ID they designated, and perfectly match the last digits of that number each time they vote. This means another hoop to jump through, and voters can easily get tripped up if they write the wrong digits or provide a signature but not the ID number. And Prop. 39 doesn’t provide a way for voters to fix these simple mistakes — or even receive notice — before their ballot is thrown out.
Citizenship is already required for federal, state and almost all California local elections. What is objectionable about asking officials to use government data to make “best efforts” to verify that registered voters are citizens?
Citizenship is already a voting requirement in the California Constitution. Anyone registering to vote must swear, under penalty of perjury, that they’re a U.S. citizen. California keeps a statewide registration system and regularly checks the rolls against reliable databases. Prop. 39 is adding another layer of “citizenship checks” that would mistakenly flag some naturalized citizens as noncitizens, especially since no comprehensive government database of U.S. citizenship exists. Recent ProPublica reporting on similar checks using Trump’s SAVE database revealed that this could yield an “ungodly” number of false positives (https://www.propublica.org/article/noncitizen-voting-trump-homeland-security-investigations). Prop. 39 would force a vague mandate on election workers who are already overworked and they’d have to repeat this wasteful and error-prone task annually. Before we add yet another verification layer, subject to mistake or political abuse, we need strong evidence that the current system isn’t working and that the new process won’t block eligible voters.
Prop. 39 does not specify that a voter must be removed merely because citizenship cannot be verified through government data. Are opponents distinguishing between what the measure expressly requires and what future implementing legislation might require?
Prop. 39 doesn’t mandate removing a voter just because their citizenship couldn’t be confirmed — but the concern is implementation. Experts agree that there is no complete, accurate list of who is and isn’t a U.S. citizen, which means any fishing expedition conducted because of Prop. 39 would result in error-filled reports. This fuels confusion, disinformation and mistrust in our elections, giving ammunition to bad actors who want eligible voters purged from the rolls. Prop. 39 also lets private actors sue elections officials, forcing underresourced local governments to choose between caving to demands for overly aggressive voter purges and spending taxpayer money to defend against frivolous litigation. Because so many details are left open, future changes or court cases could create new problems for voters flagged by the process. So, it’s not just about what’s written in Prop. 39; it’s also about the uncertainty it creates down the line.
The measure requires annual reporting of the percentage of registered voters whose citizenship has been verified and biennial state auditor reviews of state and county compliance. Do you oppose those requirements themselves, or primarily their cost and connection to the identification mandate?
We’re concerned about both. California already requires voters to swear they’re citizens and has proven systems to check registration information and keep the rolls up to date. Prop. 39 would add redundant, wasteful and potentially dangerous mandates to the work of our trusted and under-resourced elections officials without showing that the current system is broken. It would also require ongoing reporting and audits, which could cost state and local governments tens or even hundreds of millions of dollars each year, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office. We should be asking whether these costs actually solve a real problem before making taxpayers and county election officials pay the price.
If your objection is that Prop. 39 leaves critical protections to future legislation, would you support a narrower law that specifies broadly acceptable ID, provisional voting, advance notice and a guaranteed opportunity to correct errors? If not, is your objection to this measure’s drafting or to voter ID requirements generally?
The main issue is that Prop. 39’s new requirements would create unnecessary new hurdles for eligible voters and new ways to reject valid ballots, without offering any evidence that there’s a problem it would solve. Voter participation rates in the U.S. are already amongst the lowest for many industrialized countries. We also have concerns about how Prop. 39 is written since it leaves many important details to future laws, like which IDs would be accepted, whether mail voters would get notice or a chance to fix mistakes with their ID number, and what counts as “best efforts” for citizenship checks. The Legislative Analyst’s Office provided a large cost-estimate range because so much is left undefined in Prop. 39. Election laws should keep voting secure without making it harder for people who have the right to vote.
What do proponents of this get most wrong?
Proponents get two big things wrong. First, California’s elections are already safe and secure, with strong systems for checking voter registration and keeping the rolls accurate and up to date. Second, Prop. 39 would fundamentally change how we vote; more than 80% of Californians voted by mail in the 2024 presidential election. Prop. 39 would force those voters to add the last four digits of a specific ID number to their ballot envelope, creating the risk of ballot rejection for simple errors and exposing them to identity theft. It would add new ID requirements for in-person voters and subject all voters to repeated, faulty citizenship checks. This isn’t just a small administrative tweak; it’s a major change, backed by MAGA billionaires (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316461529.html) and demanded by President Trump, who called for it as a precondition for California receiving federal aid after the 2025 Southern California wildfires. That context matters here.

Would Prop 39 speed up or slow down California’s vote-counting?
By Sara DiNatale (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/sara-dinatale/) , Staff Writer Oct 11, 2026
Marion Gautier helps organize and count absentee and mail-in ballots at the San Francisco Department of Elections at City Hall on Nov. 6, 2019.
Gabrielle Lurie/S.F. Chronicle
Most of the conservatives who critique California’s election system have two separate complaints: They believe California’s vote-counting process is riddled with fraud, and they think the state takes far too long to count its votes. (Many say that the latter is evidence of the former.)
Backers of Proposition 39, a measure to implement voter ID requirements, say their plan will solve both issues. Experts, however, say the measure’s requirements would slow down, not speed up, vote-counting.

Prop 39 would require voters to show government-issued identification each time they cast a ballot in person. People who vote by mail would have to register a PIN that’s either the last four digits of their Social Security number or their driver’s license number. They could also request a free “voter ID” with a number on it. The number would need to be handwritten on the ballot envelope. Election offices would then have to check and verify the number. Critics say that means essentially 26 million people would have to reregister to vote across California.
The proposition’s cocreator, Assembly Member Carl DeMaio, R-San Diego, has cast Prop 39 as a simple and necessary change to fortify voters’ trust in state elections. During a May episode of his podcast, DeMaio said the measure’s requirement of a four-digit PIN would replace the signature verification process for the more than 80% of voters using mail-in ballots. He said that if Prop 39 becomes law, mail-in ballots would be processed “literally within 48 hours of them coming back.”
Meredith Shields, the press secretary for the Yes on 39 campaign, reiterated those claims in a statement on Friday, saying “providing a four-digit PIN when voting by mail, election officials will not have to match electronic signatures.”
But the measure does not contain any language about the PIN numbers usurping signature verification, which is codified in state law. That means the new handwritten PINs would be required and verified in addition to signatures, not in lieu of them, voting experts said.

The state’s official voter guide lays out what a yes vote means: “Voters would be required to present additional identifying information to elections officials each time they vote” — language that suggests the PIN is an extra layer of verification, not a replacement.
“Voters can read the language of Prop 39 for themselves,” said Brittany Stonesifer, an attorney and voting rights advocate with nonprofit California Common Cause. “It would add additional requirements for mail ballots. It says nothing about removing the existing signature verification process.”
DeMaio suggested during his podcast that there would be a “scanning” system for the PIN numbers, but that would require infrastructure and technology that election offices don’t yet have.
“The notion that this will speed up the process is asinine,” said Stephen Richer, a Republican former recorder of Maricopa County, Ariz. “I don’t know how having an additional requirement could possibly make the process go faster.”
Richer said he broadly supports ID checks at polling places to verify that the person trying to vote matches the person recorded in the voter rolls. California doesn’t do that. Voters must present a government ID when they register to vote, but when voting in person they only must provide poll workers with their name and address, and sign a voter roster.

“It would absolutely result in valid mail ballots being rejected, potentially at a high level, with no evidence that it would increase security,” Stonesifer said of the four-digit PIN numbers.
Assembly Member Gail Pellerin, D-Santa Cruz, who is the head of the Assembly Elections Committee and a former elections official, agrees. She told the Los Angeles Times (https://www.latimes.com/california/newsletter/2026-09-28/skelton-monday-politics-newsletter-voter-id) that under Prop 39, not only would some voters’ ballots be rejected by mistake but the measure would “absolutely” slow down counting.
Richer, Stonesifer, Pellerin and other voting experts largely agree signature verification is a secure and efficient way to vet mail-in ballots. Some election offices use software to quickly confirm a signature match and kick any questionable ones to workers who can pull up someone’s state signature history to see how it may have changed over time.
If the signature still looks odd, they notify the voter it needs to be fixed. California has a long window allowing ballot curing, which is a common criticism of the state’s lagging vote-tallying process. But legislation just signed into law by Gov. Gavin Newsom requires all counties to allow digital signature curing in order to speed the process.
Shields, the Prop 39 campaign spokesperson, said the measure would not only speed the process, but would conserve resources.

“When Prop 39 passes, IDs will be free of charge and the verification and counting of ballots will be faster, more accurate, and will save election officials valuable time and resources,” she said.
The state’s nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, however, estimates the measure would cost the state and local governments tens of millions to hundreds of millions of dollars. Darius Kemp, the director of Common Cause California, said the measure would also take resources away from counties and clerks, impeding them from counting more quickly.
Pamela Smith, president of Verified Voting, a nonprofit focused on election security, said that if someone was so determined to cheat that they would spoof a signature, there’s no reason to believe they wouldn’t also pilfer a PIN. She, too, was wary that the measure would speed up the count.
“The costs to taxpayers associated with implementation are significant, which might not matter if this were a game changer for efficiency or security, but it is neither,” Smith said.
Prop 39 does not include a curing process for PIN codes.

State Sen. Jesse Arreguín, D-Berkeley, also argued the measure will impede in-person voting.
“Repetitive ID checks under Prop 39 are not only unnecessary, they will slow our checking and create longer lines and delays for people to vote and make it harder for them to participate in their right to vote,” Arreguín said during the Friday rally in Oakland.
Stonesifer said funding more staffers in election offices — rather than implementing a new system to scan four-digit codes — would be a better way to speed up the counting process.
DeMaio and his critics do agree on one thing: They’re all encouraging voters to return their ballots early. One of the biggest factors that slows California’s tabulation is the surge of vote-by-mail ballots returned on Election Day.

Would Prop 39 speed up or slow down California’s vote-counting?
By Sara DiNatale (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/sara-dinatale/) , Staff Writer Oct 11, 2026
Marion Gautier helps organize and count absentee and mail-in ballots at the San Francisco Department of Elections at City Hall on Nov. 6, 2019.
Gabrielle Lurie/S.F. Chronicle
Most of the conservatives who critique California’s election system have two separate complaints: They believe California’s vote-counting process is riddled with fraud, and they think the state takes far too long to count its votes. (Many say that the latter is evidence of the former.)
Backers of Proposition 39, a measure to implement voter ID requirements, say their plan will solve both issues. Experts, however, say the measure’s requirements would slow down, not speed up, vote-counting.
Chronicle endorsements: Editorial Board’s recommendations for 2026 election (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2026/california-sf-election-endorsements/)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 39 would require voters to show government-issued identification each time they cast a ballot in person. People who vote by mail would have to register a PIN that’s either the last four digits of their Social Security number or their driver’s license number. They could also request a free “voter ID” with a number on it. The number would need to be handwritten on the ballot envelope. Election offices would then have to check and verify the number. Critics say that means essentially 26 million people would have to reregister to vote across California.
The proposition’s cocreator, Assembly Member Carl DeMaio, R-San Diego, has cast Prop 39 as a simple and necessary change to fortify voters’ trust in state elections. During a May episode of his podcast, DeMaio said the measure’s requirement of a four-digit PIN would replace the signature verification process for the more than 80% of voters using mail-in ballots. He said that if Prop 39 becomes law, mail-in ballots would be processed “literally within 48 hours of them coming back.”
Meredith Shields, the press secretary for the Yes on 39 campaign, reiterated those claims in a statement on Friday, saying “providing a four-digit PIN when voting by mail, election officials will not have to match electronic signatures.”
But the measure does not contain any language about the PIN numbers usurping signature verification, which is codified in state law. That means the new handwritten PINs would be required and verified in addition to signatures, not in lieu of them, voting experts said.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
The state’s official voter guide lays out what a yes vote means: “Voters would be required to present additional identifying information to elections officials each time they vote” — language that suggests the PIN is an extra layer of verification, not a replacement.
“Voters can read the language of Prop 39 for themselves,” said Brittany Stonesifer, an attorney and voting rights advocate with nonprofit California Common Cause. “It would add additional requirements for mail ballots. It says nothing about removing the existing signature verification process.”
DeMaio suggested during his podcast that there would be a “scanning” system for the PIN numbers, but that would require infrastructure and technology that election offices don’t yet have.
“The notion that this will speed up the process is asinine,” said Stephen Richer, a Republican former recorder of Maricopa County, Ariz. “I don’t know how having an additional requirement could possibly make the process go faster.”
Richer said he broadly supports ID checks at polling places to verify that the person trying to vote matches the person recorded in the voter rolls. California doesn’t do that. Voters must present a government ID when they register to vote, but when voting in person they only must provide poll workers with their name and address, and sign a voter roster.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
“It would absolutely result in valid mail ballots being rejected, potentially at a high level, with no evidence that it would increase security,” Stonesifer said of the four-digit PIN numbers.
Assembly Member Gail Pellerin, D-Santa Cruz, who is the head of the Assembly Elections Committee and a former elections official, agrees. She told the Los Angeles Times (https://www.latimes.com/california/newsletter/2026-09-28/skelton-monday-politics-newsletter-voter-id) that under Prop 39, not only would some voters’ ballots be rejected by mistake but the measure would “absolutely” slow down counting.
Richer, Stonesifer, Pellerin and other voting experts largely agree signature verification is a secure and efficient way to vet mail-in ballots. Some election offices use software to quickly confirm a signature match and kick any questionable ones to workers who can pull up someone’s state signature history to see how it may have changed over time.
If the signature still looks odd, they notify the voter it needs to be fixed. California has a long window allowing ballot curing, which is a common criticism of the state’s lagging vote-tallying process. But legislation just signed into law by Gov. Gavin Newsom requires all counties to allow digital signature curing in order to speed the process.
Shields, the Prop 39 campaign spokesperson, said the measure would not only speed the process, but would conserve resources.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
“When Prop 39 passes, IDs will be free of charge and the verification and counting of ballots will be faster, more accurate, and will save election officials valuable time and resources,” she said.
The state’s nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, however, estimates the measure would cost the state and local governments tens of millions to hundreds of millions of dollars. Darius Kemp, the director of Common Cause California, said the measure would also take resources away from counties and clerks, impeding them from counting more quickly.
Pamela Smith, president of Verified Voting, a nonprofit focused on election security, said that if someone was so determined to cheat that they would spoof a signature, there’s no reason to believe they wouldn’t also pilfer a PIN. She, too, was wary that the measure would speed up the count.
“The costs to taxpayers associated with implementation are significant, which might not matter if this were a game changer for efficiency or security, but it is neither,” Smith said.
Prop 39 does not include a curing process for PIN codes.

“My mother has very interesting handwriting,” Rep. Lateefah Simon, D-Oakland, said during a Friday rally against Prop 39. “If, in fact, the registrar of voters cannot read her handwriting or her Social Security number ... what will happen to her ballot? It will be discarded.”
State Sen. Jesse Arreguín, D-Berkeley, also argued the measure will impede in-person voting.
“Repetitive ID checks under Prop 39 are not only unnecessary, they will slow our checking and create longer lines and delays for people to vote and make it harder for them to participate in their right to vote,” Arreguín said during the Friday rally in Oakland.
Stonesifer said funding more staffers in election offices — rather than implementing a new system to scan four-digit codes — would be a better way to speed up the counting process.
DeMaio and his critics do agree on one thing: They’re all encouraging voters to return their ballots early. One of the biggest factors that slows California’s tabulation is the surge of vote-by-mail ballots returned on Election Day.

Some election offices use software to quickly confirm a signature match and kick any questionable ones to workers who can pull up someone’s state signature history to see how it may have changed over time.
If the signature still looks odd, they notify the voter it needs to be fixed. California has a long window allowing ballot curing, which is a common criticism of the state’s lagging vote-tallying process. But legislation just signed into law by Gov. Gavin Newsom requires all counties to allow digital signature curing in order to speed the process.
Shields, the Prop 39 campaign spokesperson, said the measure would not only speed the process, but would conserve resources.

“When Prop 39 passes, IDs will be free of charge and the verification and counting of ballots will be faster, more accurate, and will save election officials valuable time and resources,” she said.
The state’s nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, however, estimates the measure would cost the state and local governments tens of millions to hundreds of millions of dollars. Darius Kemp, the director of Common Cause California, said the measure would also take resources away from counties and clerks, impeding them from counting more quickly.
Pamela Smith, president of Verified Voting, a nonprofit focused on election security, said that if someone was so determined to cheat that they would spoof a signature, there’s no reason to believe they wouldn’t also pilfer a PIN. She, too, was wary that the measure would speed up the count.
“The costs to taxpayers associated with implementation are significant, which might not matter if this were a game changer for efficiency or security, but it is neither,” Smith said.
Prop 39 does not include a curing process for PIN codes.

Would Prop 39 speed up or slow down California’s vote-counting?
By Sara DiNatale (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/sara-dinatale/) , Staff Writer Oct 11, 2026
Marion Gautier helps organize and count absentee and mail-in ballots at the San Francisco Department of Elections at City Hall on Nov. 6, 2019.
Gabrielle Lurie/S.F. Chronicle
Most of the conservatives who critique California’s election system have two separate complaints: They believe California’s vote-counting process is riddled with fraud, and they think the state takes far too long to count its votes. (Many say that the latter is evidence of the former.)
Backers of Proposition 39, a measure to implement voter ID requirements, say their plan will solve both issues. Experts, however, say the measure’s requirements would slow down, not speed up, vote-counting.
Chronicle endorsements: Editorial Board’s recommendations for 2026 election (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2026/california-sf-election-endorsements/)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 39 would require voters to show government-issued identification each time they cast a ballot in person. People who vote by mail would have to register a PIN that’s either the last four digits of their Social Security number or their driver’s license number. They could also request a free “voter ID” with a number on it. The number would need to be handwritten on the ballot envelope. Election offices would then have to check and verify the number. Critics say that means essentially 26 million people would have to reregister to vote across California.
The proposition’s cocreator, Assembly Member Carl DeMaio, R-San Diego, has cast Prop 39 as a simple and necessary change to fortify voters’ trust in state elections. During a May episode of his podcast, DeMaio said the measure’s requirement of a four-digit PIN would replace the signature verification process for the more than 80% of voters using mail-in ballots. He said that if Prop 39 becomes law, mail-in ballots would be processed “literally within 48 hours of them coming back.”
Meredith Shields, the press secretary for the Yes on 39 campaign, reiterated those claims in a statement on Friday, saying “providing a four-digit PIN when voting by mail, election officials will not have to match electronic signatures.”
But the measure does not contain any language about the PIN numbers usurping signature verification, which is codified in state law. That means the new handwritten PINs would be required and verified in addition to signatures, not in lieu of them, voting experts said.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
The state’s official voter guide lays out what a yes vote means: “Voters would be required to present additional identifying information to elections officials each time they vote” — language that suggests the PIN is an extra layer of verification, not a replacement.
“Voters can read the language of Prop 39 for themselves,” said Brittany Stonesifer, an attorney and voting rights advocate with nonprofit California Common Cause. “It would add additional requirements for mail ballots. It says nothing about removing the existing signature verification process.”
DeMaio suggested during his podcast that there would be a “scanning” system for the PIN numbers, but that would require infrastructure and technology that election offices don’t yet have.
“The notion that this will speed up the process is asinine,” said Stephen Richer, a Republican former recorder of Maricopa County, Ariz. “I don’t know how having an additional requirement could possibly make the process go faster.”
Richer said he broadly supports ID checks at polling places to verify that the person trying to vote matches the person recorded in the voter rolls. California doesn’t do that. Voters must present a government ID when they register to vote, but when voting in person they only must provide poll workers with their name and address, and sign a voter roster.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
“It would absolutely result in valid mail ballots being rejected, potentially at a high level, with no evidence that it would increase security,” Stonesifer said of the four-digit PIN numbers.
Assembly Member Gail Pellerin, D-Santa Cruz, who is the head of the Assembly Elections Committee and a former elections official, agrees. She told the Los Angeles Times (https://www.latimes.com/california/newsletter/2026-09-28/skelton-monday-politics-newsletter-voter-id) that under Prop 39, not only would some voters’ ballots be rejected by mistake but the measure would “absolutely” slow down counting.
Richer, Stonesifer, Pellerin and other voting experts largely agree signature verification is a secure and efficient way to vet mail-in ballots. Some election offices use software to quickly confirm a signature match and kick any questionable ones to workers who can pull up someone’s state signature history to see how it may have changed over time.
If the signature still looks odd, they notify the voter it needs to be fixed. California has a long window allowing ballot curing, which is a common criticism of the state’s lagging vote-tallying process. But legislation just signed into law by Gov. Gavin Newsom requires all counties to allow digital signature curing in order to speed the process.
Shields, the Prop 39 campaign spokesperson, said the measure would not only speed the process, but would conserve resources.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
“When Prop 39 passes, IDs will be free of charge and the verification and counting of ballots will be faster, more accurate, and will save election officials valuable time and resources,” she said.
The state’s nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, however, estimates the measure would cost the state and local governments tens of millions to hundreds of millions of dollars. Darius Kemp, the director of Common Cause California, said the measure would also take resources away from counties and clerks, impeding them from counting more quickly.
Pamela Smith, president of Verified Voting, a nonprofit focused on election security, said that if someone was so determined to cheat that they would spoof a signature, there’s no reason to believe they wouldn’t also pilfer a PIN. She, too, was wary that the measure would speed up the count.
“The costs to taxpayers associated with implementation are significant, which might not matter if this were a game changer for efficiency or security, but it is neither,” Smith said.
Prop 39 does not include a curing process for PIN codes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
“My mother has very interesting handwriting,” Rep. Lateefah Simon, D-Oakland, said during a Friday rally against Prop 39. “If, in fact, the registrar of voters cannot read her handwriting or her Social Security number ... what will happen to her ballot? It will be discarded.”
State Sen. Jesse Arreguín, D-Berkeley, also argued the measure will impede in-person voting.
“Repetitive ID checks under Prop 39 are not only unnecessary, they will slow our checking and create longer lines and delays for people to vote and make it harder for them to participate in their right to vote,” Arreguín said during the Friday rally in Oakland.
Stonesifer said funding more staffers in election offices — rather than implementing a new system to scan four-digit codes — would be a better way to speed up the counting process.
DeMaio and his critics do agree on one thing: They’re all encouraging voters to return their ballots early. One of the biggest factors that slows California’s tabulation is the surge of vote-by-mail ballots returned on Election Day.

Sara DiNatale covers politics and the impacts of the Trump administration’s policies on the Bay Area and California. She joined the Chronicle in 2025, after a decade reporting across the southern United States for the San Antonio Express-News, the Tampa Bay Times and Mississippi Today.

# Strict Id Laws Don’t Stop Voters: Evidence from a U.S. Nationwide Panel, 2008–2018
## Abstract
U.S. states increasingly require identification to vote—an ostensible attempt to deter fraud that prompts complaints of selective disenfranchisement.
Using a difference-in-differences design on a panel data set with 1.6 billion observations, 2008–2018, we find that the laws have no negative effect on registration or turnout, overall or for any group defined by race, gender, age, or party affiliation.
These results hold through a large number of specifications.
Our most demanding specification controls for state, year, and voter fixed effects, along with state and voter time-varying controls.
Based on this specification, we obtain point estimates of −0.1 percentage points for effects both on overall registration and turnout (with 95% confidence intervals of [−2.3; 2.1 percentage points] and [−3.0; 2.8 percentage points], respectively), and +1.4 percentage points for the effect on the turnout of nonwhite voters relative to whites (with a 95% confidence interval of [−0.5; 3.2 percentage points]).
The lack of negative impact on voter turnout cannot be attributed to voters’ reaction against the laws, measured by campaign contributions and self-reported political engagement.
