By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.mercurynews.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: October 15, 2026 at 5:00 AM PDT | UPDATED: October 15, 2026 at 5:21 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
It’s impossible not to view Proposition 39 — the measure authored by Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio and backed by out-of-state, right-wing billionaires (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-election-voter-id-proposition-39/) — strictly through the lens of national politics.
In requiring voters to show IDs before receiving their ballots (among other restrictive voting rules and audits), it gives credence to President Donald Trump’s longstanding and repeatedly debunked claims that millions of noncitizens routinely vote in U.S. elections.
Related Articles
Endorsement: Break the 49ers’ grip over Santa Clara. Elect these three candidates. (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/31/endorsement-break-the-49ers-grip-over-santa-clara-make-kertes-mayor-elect-inciarte-and-crutchlow-to-council/)
Endorsement: These three City Council candidates are San Jose’s best choices (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/30/endorsement-elect-peter-ortiz-bien-doan-and-genny-altwer-to-san-jose-city-council/)
Endorsement: Elect Michael Melillo to San Jose Unified School District Board of Education (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/30/endorsement-elect-michael-melillo-to-san-jose-unified-school-district-board-of-education/)
Endorsement: Reject San Mateo Community College District’s $848 million Measure V (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-reject-san-mateo-community-college-districts-848-million-measure-v/)
Endorsement: Voters should support the Measure M bond to fix Gilroy schools (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-voters-should-support-the-measure-m-bond-to-fix-gilroy-schools/)
This initiative is an expensive solution to a phantom problem. Reject Prop. 39.
Manufactured crisis
Multiple groups have studied the issue and found scant evidence of widespread fraud. The California State Library (https://www.library.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/crb-reports/CRB-Voter-Fraud-Presentation-Senate-Elections-2026-04-03.pdf) looked at 14 counties where grand juries issued reports on the risk of voter fraud in the 2020, 2022 and 2024 elections and found secure elections everywhere. The Brennan Center for Justice’s research confirmed that voter fraud is a myth (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/debunking-voter-fraud-myth). Even the conservative Heritage Foundation could only find 71 instances (https://electionfraud.heritage.org/search?case_type=All&fraud_type=All&state=CA) of voter fraud in California — over more than four decades. Also, California already takes election integrity (https://abc7news.com/post/150000-mail-ballots-rejected-californias-primary-despite-efforts-count-every-vote/19571066/) seriously, which is one reason our process of confirming elections is so slow (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/17/upshot/california-slow-election-results.html).
RELATED: Endorsement Cheat Sheet: Mercury News and East Bay Times Editorial Boards’ top picks for California’s Nov. 3 general election (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/13/bay-area-news-group-california-election-endorsements-november-2026/)
Our editorial board repeatedly asked the Yes on Prop. 39 campaign for evidence of voter fraud in California, rampant or otherwise, and they deflected, dodged and denied the premise of our questions. They insisted that fraud wasn’t actually the issue — that Prop. 39 is about improving public trust and confidence in our democracy.
So it’s purely coincidence that Donald Trump demanded “voter ID” laws in California as a condition for wildfire disaster relief (https://abc7.com/post/president-donald-trump-wants-voter-id-laws-condition-aid-california/15833908/) last year. Or that the measure’s biggest backer, Illinois billionaire Richard Uihlein, has a history ofcontributing (https://www.propublica.org/article/uline-uihlein-election-denial) to the campaigns of election deniers.
According to the Public Policy Institute of California (https://data.ddhq.io/polls/2026/05/30/Public-Policy-Institute-of-California-California), a quarter of likely voters are very concerned that it’s too easy for ineligible people to vote. That’s not zero, but it also doesn’t mean we should be changing election laws to accommodate the fact-free fears of a minority of Californians.
In other polls about trust in our elections, it is overwhelmingly Republicans who are the most concerned. That’s fine. But if they really cared about improving those numbers, we’d recommend they start by asking the president to stop spreading false information.
We absolutely wouldn’t recommend, as Prop. 39 does, that private citizens be allowed to sue if they believe the government isn’t complying with the measure’s rules. We don’t even want to imagine the kind of frivolous litigation that could inspire.
Why panic?
It’s possible to view Prop. 39 and say, “What’s the big deal?” Thirty-six statesrequire (https://ballotpedia.org/Voter_identification_laws_by_state) voters to present identification before voting in person.
Well, the big deal is that a lot of eligible people might not be able to vote if the measure is passed. Millions of Californians (https://cdce.umd.edu/sites/cdce.umd.edu/files/Who%20Lacks%20ID%20and%20Proof%20of%20Citizenship%20in%20California%20Today_.pdf) wouldn’t have the ID required to satisfy this proposal. (They’d have to request a new one.) And, as the No on Prop. 39 campaign pointed out to us, when Texas implemented similar mail-ballot ID rules, rejections shot up (https://www.texastribune.org/2022/04/06/texas-mail-in-ballot-rejection-voting/) from 1% to 12%.
Plus, completely revamping the voter verification system will come with financial costs — “between tens of millions of dollars and low hundreds of millions of dollars each year,” according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office.
Prop. 39 isn’t just about voter ID. It contains a provision that is deeply problematic: requiring election officials to use their “best efforts” to verify the citizenship status of voters they register, with regular audits to ensure compliance.
But there is no reliable government list of U.S. citizens. The Supreme Court decided that the federal government could continue to try to create one, but it’s already full of mistakes (https://www.npr.org/2026/09/25/nx-s1-5976804/supreme-court-trump-save-noncitizen-voting), labeling many citizens as ineligible to vote.
This deeply flawed measure would create chaos for no reason.
Reject Prop. 39.

Should California require voter and citizenship ID? Our Prop. 39 endorsement | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated September 30, 2026 2:30 PM
Ballots are dropped off at a polling location on Fountain Square Drive in Citrus Heights on Election Day, June 2, 2026. On November ballots in California, Prop. 39 seeks to require more identification from Californians before they vote.
JOSÉ LUIS VILLEGAS
jvillegas@sacbee.com
Proposition 39 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317005401.html) promises to tighten California’s elections and reduce the likelihood of voter fraud. However, the measure creates more barriers than it removes, threatening to disenfranchise legitimate voters.
Prop. 39, if passed, would change California’s voting laws by requiring voters to show government-issued identification before voting in person. For mail ballots, voters would need to provide the last four digits of a government-issued ID number, such as a driver’s license number, when submitting their ballots.
It would also require state and local elections officials to make “best efforts” using government data to verify that voters are U.S. citizens. Additionally, the state would be required to issue free identification cards to voters who do not already have a qualifying ID.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 39 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317005401.html)
In practice, Prop. 39 would add a new ID requirement to safeguards California already has, resulting in more legitimate ballots being rejected than fraudulent votes being prevented.
For this reason and others, the collective editorial boards of The Sacramento Bee, (https://www.sacbee.com/)Modesto Bee, (https://www.modbee.com/) Merced Sun-Star, (https://www.mercedsunstar.com/) Fresno Bee (https://www.fresnobee.com/) and San Luis Obispo Tribune (https://www.sanluisobispo.com/) urge a “no” vote on Prop. 39.
“The vast majority of registrars across the state, and that includes the Sacramento area, are doing a really good job with the tools we already have in place,” said Justin Levitt, a law professor at Loyola Law School. (https://www.lls.edu/) Levitt opposes Prop. 39, as do many prominent Democrats in California. (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316925218.html)
Federal law already requires new voters who register remotely to prove who they are through documents such as a driver’s license or passport, (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/hava-id-standards) under the Help America Vote Act, (https://www.eac.gov/about/help_america_vote_act.aspx) passed by Congress in 2002.
Julia Gomez, a staff attorney with the ACLU of Southern California who opposes Prop. 39, warns that adding another technical requirement to mail-in ballots only makes the process more difficult.
“For the June primary, county election officials rejected nearly 44,000 mail-in ballots because a voter’s signature did not match the signature on file, and more than 8,000 were rejected because the envelope lacked a signature,” Gomez noted. “That just means the voter forgot to sign the envelope. That’s 8,000 disenfranchised voters.”
Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, R-San Diego, is one of two Republican legislators behind Prop. 39. The other is state Sen. Tony Strickland, R-Huntington Beach. As The Bee reported, Prop. 39 has attracted the attention of several conservative billionaires who have invested heavily in Prop. 39.
“Backers of Proposition 39, which would also require voters to show proof of U.S. citizenship when registering to vote, raised more than $10 million so far,” wrote The Bee’s Ben Paviour in July. “At least nine billionaires, as tracked by Forbes’ list, have invested in the fundraising committee Californians for Voter ID, which is run by Julie Luckey, the mother of tech billionaire and President Donald Trump supporter Palmer Luckey.”
Supporters of Prop. 39 tout it as a vehicle to enhance voting protections in California.
“A lot of people are sick and tired of the conspiracy theories and don’t want to have low public trust and confidence in elections, and they see voter ID as the common sense bipartisan way to fix it,” DeMaio said in Paviour’s July story. “Why is that such a mystery?”
It’s not a mystery at all. Prop. 39 is bad policy.
“A voter can accidentally leave that space blank,” Gomez said. “ They can enter the wrong number. They can transpose digits, or they can simply not understand what the instructions say.”
California doesn’t have a voter fraud crisis. It has a trust crisis, fueled by national politicians — most notably Trump—who lost elections and invented conspiracies to explain it.
We urge Californians to vote “no” on Prop. 39.

Endorsement: Prop 39 would create CEQA for voting rights. No thanks
Even if you think voter fraud is a problem in California (it’s not), Prop 39 would turn our elections into a never-ending lawsuit
Proposition 39 would require Californians to present or incorporate some form of identification when voting. It is almost certain to disenfranchise eligible voters. The Chronicle’s editorial board recommends a no vote.
Todd Trumbull/S.F. Chronicle from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 12, 2026
Is voter fraud rampant in California?
A May poll by the Public Policy Institute of California (https://data.ddhq.io/polls/2026/05/30/Public-Policy-Institute-of-California-California) found that 41% of likely voters here were either “very” or “somewhat” concerned that it’s too easy for ineligible voters to cast ballots.
That’s not an insignificant number.

So, how can California shore up trust?
Carl DeMaio, the firebrand Republican Assembly member from San Diego, claims to have the answer: Proposition 39 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf).
The measure would create a host of new voter-identification requirements in California and mandate regular election audits. Prop 39 was placed on the November ballot via a signature-gathering effort by volunteers from DeMaio’s advocacy organization (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/02/carl-demaio-california-maga-voter-id-prop-39-01103730?nname=california-playbook&nid=00000150-384f-da43-aff2-bf7fd35a0000&nrid=adfb3333-039f-4cee-9cbe-7aea15435a8e), Reform California, and paid operatives funded by Julie Luckey (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook-pm/2025/11/24/the-donor-powering-a-voter-id-push-in-california-00667090), whose son Palmer was recently named as a leader of the Trump administration’s new Project Meridian war council (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/openforum/article/pentagon-weapon-military-war-22464710.php).
Even though wealthy out-of-state Republicans have largely funded the yes campaign, DeMaio inexplicably insisted to the editorial board that the measure is “a balanced, bipartisan approach.”

Prop 39 is “the best way to shut down the conspiracy theories that irresponsible politicians spread,” DeMaio said.
Well, no.
The best way is for those irresponsible politicians, paramount among them DeMaio’s ally, President Donald Trump, to stop sowing unfounded disbelief.
Because by every available measure, California’s voting system is working.
The California State Library’s research bureau examined reports from 14 counties (https://www.library.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/crb-reports/CRB-Voter-Fraud-Presentation-Senate-Elections-2026-04-03.pdf) where grand juries investigated voter fraud risks from 2020 to 2024 and found an overwhelming consensus: no evidence of systemic or significant fraud. Even the right-wing Heritage Foundation — the organization behind Project 2025 — identified just 71 instances of known voter fraud in California (https://electionfraud.heritage.org/search?case_type=All&fraud_type=All&state=CA) from 1982 to 2025.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
All of those cases were prosecuted — evidence that California takes election integrity seriously. In fact, the state rejected its highest percentage of mail ballots in more than a decade (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/california-mail-ballot-rejections-22359196.php) for the June 2 primary — largely because they were postmarked after Election Day or arrived too late. There was also an uptick in signatures that election officials couldn’t verify.
Yet Prop 39 supporters insist on the need for additional identity verification.
To understand Prop 39’s proposed changes and the impact, let’s first look at the state’s existing processes:
Under California law (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration), anyone registering to vote must prove their identity via their driver’s license, state identification number or the last four digits of their Social Security number. Election officials check this identification against state and federal databases. Voters must also attest under penalty of perjury — which carries a potential prison sentence — that they’re a U.S. citizen living in California who’s at least 18 years old and not currently in prison or found incapable of voting by a court.
Every registered voter in California then receives a mail-in ballot, which most residents prefer (more than 80% voted this way in the past election). Before counting it, election officials check whether the voter’s signature on the outside of the ballot matches the signature on file (usually from a driver’s license). If it doesn’t, election officials give voters a chance to “cure” it by notifying them of the issue and providing a correction form (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/statewide-elections/2026-general/november-3-2026-general-combo-statement.pdf), which they have 22 days to return.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
People voting in person typically don’t have to present ID, but they do have to sign a registration list at the polls.
Prop 39 would change all that. To vote by mail, Californians would have to preselect a form of government-issued identification and write the last four digits of that ID on the outside of their ballot.
To vote in person, Californians would need to show a government-issued ID. Prop 39 mandates the state provide free “voter identification cards” — which do not currently exist — to those who request them. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop39-110326.pdf) estimated that creating these cards, in addition to other expenses resulting from Prop 39, could cost local and state governments hundreds of millions of dollars a year.
The measure also requires state and local elections officials to employ “best efforts” to verify registered voters are U.S. citizens and to publish annual reports revealing the percentage of verified voters. It mandates the state auditor to review compliance every other year.
What forms of government-issued ID would be acceptable under Prop 39, and how would voters preselect the ID they want to use for their 4-digit PIN? Do they get a chance to cure their ballots if they write the wrong digits on their vote-by-mail envelope? And what would be considered “best efforts” to verify someone’s citizenship status — given that even the federal government doesn’t have a comprehensive list of citizens?

Article continues below this ad
Prop 39 directs the state Legislature to “promptly” enact laws to answer these questions. It also creates a private right of action that permits any person who believes state or local government isn’t complying with the measure to take those entities to court.
Justin Levitt, a constitutional and election law expert at the Loyola Law School, called this a “generic litigation trap” that opens the door to countless frivolous lawsuits.
Just as the California Environmental Quality Act enables aggrieved NIMBYs to weaponize the legal system against development projects they dislike, Prop 39 will do the same with elections.
“You will have plenty of advocacy organizations that are eager to sue over perceived noncompliance with this initiative early and often,” Levitt told the editorial board.
And Prop 39 is almost certain to disenfranchise eligible voters.
Large numbers of California U.S. citizens lack either IDs or proof of citizenship. A 2026 University of Maryland analysis (https://cdce.umd.edu/sites/cdce.umd.edu/files/Who%20Lacks%20ID%20and%20Proof%20of%20Citizenship%20in%20California%20Today_.pdf) found that about 2.7 million Californians, or about 11% of eligible voters, don’t have a driver’s license, while 13% have one that’s expired or has an outdated address or name. People of color, young residents, disabled Californians and lower-income residents are disproportionately represented in these groups.
The study also found 24% of Californians don’t have a passport and that more than 3 million voting-age Californians would have difficulty readily accessing documents proving their citizenship.
In short, Prop 39 would do little to stop the minimal fraud that exists while creating millions “more chances for valid ballots to be rejected,” Abdi Soltani, executive director of ACLU of Northern California, told the editorial board.
After Texas passed a similar voter-ID law in 2021, its rate of rejected ballots skyrocketed from less than 1% to more than 12% (https://www.texastribune.org/2022/04/06/texas-mail-in-ballot-rejection-voting/), effectively invalidating 1 in 8 votes cast in the 2022 primary. A peer-reviewed study (https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/737439) found it also reduced voter turnout in subsequent elections.

California could do more to assuage concerns about election integrity. Counties have been begging the state for permission to join a nonprofit, multistate organization that helps officials improve the accuracy of their voter rolls (https://apcp.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2024-04/ab-2050-pellerin-apcp-analysis_1.pdf).
But Prop 39 is a nakedly bad-faith effort designed to encourage frivolous lawsuits, deepen distrust, increase political polarization and waste taxpayer dollars. Vote no.

I've got the editorial board pieces in hand, so next I'm looking for the PPIC September 2026 survey and other polling, plus the empirical voter ID research: Cantoni and Pons on strict ID laws, and the newer peer-reviewed study on Texas SB1 that the Chronicle cited.

Next I'm checking who the editorial pieces are from, then looking at the LA Times explainer, the opposing CalMatters commentary, and the state library's voter fraud report. I also want to see whether the rollout rules say how existing voters would designate their ID, and what legal challenges are expected.

Now I'm weighing the federal materiality provision for paper errors, which courts have applied to mail ballot date and ID number requirements. The Fifth Circuit reversed a 2023 ruling on Texas's mail ballot ID number rule, so I want to see how the Ninth Circuit is likely to treat it.

I'm checking how rejection rates for mail ballots in Texas dropped from about 12.4% in the March 2022 primary to roughly 2.7% in the November 2022 general, and whether 2024 went lower still. I want sources for those numbers. I'm also glancing at the Huntington Beach Measure A situation and SB 1174, which look like background, and a breaking story about the Supreme Court and California ballots that may not bear directly on this. Next I'm searching for the PPIC survey.

Key Findings
The California election has entered its final stretch, with the governor’s race at the top of the ticket and 52 House races that will help determine the party in control of the 120th Congress. The November 3 ballot also includes 14 state propositions—five legislative measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—the most since the November 2016 election. The 2025–26 legislative session ended in late August with a flurry of bills sent to Governor Newsom to sign or veto in September. The recent trends in job growth, consumer prices, and interest rates send mixed signals about the US and California economy.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey on topics including the November races, legislative ballot measures, and citizens’ initiatives, as well as state and national issues that was conducted September 4–September 10, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) continues to lead Steve Hilton (R) by a wide margin (60% to 38%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a similarly wide margin (62% to 36%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty-five percent say that the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote. Fifty-eight percent say that voting is more important this year than in past midterms. After reading the ballot titles and labels, majorities would vote yes on Proposition 1 (55%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (60%; Rainy Day Fund). Three other legislative ballot measures fall short of a majority.
Fifty-two percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would also vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (61%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (55%; Immunology Bond), Proposition 41 (51%; Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), and Proposition 42 (54%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Partisans vary in their support for these citizens’ initiatives. Three other citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Overwhelming majorities agree that there are too many propositions on the state ballot.
Majorities of adults and likely voters think that the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Fifty-one percent of adults and likely voters say that they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance, while 45 percent of adults and 48 percent of likely voters approve of the state legislature. Majorities of adults and likely voters report that recent price increases have caused financial hardships for their household. Seventy percent of Californians think that the state is divided into economic groups, the haves and have-nots. Majorities of adults and likely voters say that they can trust the state government in Sacramento to do what is right “only some of the time.”
Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-three percent of adults and 27 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance, while 17 percent of adults and 16 percent of likely voters approve of the US Congress. Seven in ten Californians are dissatisfied with the availability of affordable health care and believe that the US government is responsible for ensuring that all Americans have access to health care. Fewer than half say the major parties have a lot or some good ideas. Overwhelming majorities say they can trust the federal government to do what is right “only some of the time.”
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
The top two vote-getters in the California June primary for statewide elected offices and for federal and state legislative seats are on the November ballot. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom, who is termed out of office. There are 52 House races in California that will help determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will also decide on 14 state propositions this fall—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax measures and multibillion-dollar state bonds.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a wide margin (60% to 38%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. In our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/), Becerra led Hilton by 25 points (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 93 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 92 percent of Republicans favor Hilton, while independents lean toward the Democratic candidate (57% Becerra, 38% Hilton). Majorities favor Becerra over Hilton across age, education, gender, homeownership, and income groups and in the state’s major regions except for the Central Valley (46% Becerra, 52% Hilton).
Affordability and the cost of living have been the top issue on Californians’ minds in our recent polling. Sixty-five percent of likely voters say that the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote (30% somewhat, 5% not too important). In our February survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/), the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability were very important to 61 percent of likely voters and to majorities across parties, regions, and demographic groups. Today, majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions hold this view. Notably, partisans are largely in agreement: 69 percent of Democrats, 65 percent of Republicans, and 59 percent of independents say that the gubernatorial candidates’ affordability positions are very important. Becerra supporters (66%) express this opinion as often as Hilton supporters (65%). Seven in ten or more of those who live in the Inland Empire (79%) or Los Angeles (70%), those who have incomes of $40,000 to $99,999 (74%), those who have children 18 or younger in their household (74%), Latinos (71%), renters (70%), and women (70%) say the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote.
Many Californians are watching news about the gubernatorial candidates. About six in ten likely voters say they are following news about candidates for the governor’s election either very (18%) or fairly (40%) closely. By comparison, in our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten likely voters were very (23%) or fairly closely (48%) following the news about candidates in the governor’s election, including majorities across partisan groups (68% Democrats, 76% Republicans, 65% independents) and demographic groups and regions. Similar shares were closely following the news about candidates in the gubernatorial election in September 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2018/) (21% very, 41% fairly), while fewer were in September 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2022/) (17% very, 33% fairly), and overwhelming majorities were in September 2021 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2021/) (40% very, 41% fairly) prior to the special election on the recall of Governor Newsom. Today, partisans vary in following the news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely (57% Democrats, 68% Republicans, 50% independents), as do Becerra and Hilton supporters (53% to 69%).
House Races. When asked about their House district race, most likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a wide margin (62% to 36%). Likely voter preferences were similar in July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican) and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, likely voters’ preferences for the Democratic candidate and the Republican candidate are similar in the governor’s race and the House race. More than nine in ten Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while independents say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (59% to 36%). Majorities say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district races across demographic groups and major state regions with the exception of the Central Valley (47%).
Many Californians believe that their vote matters in the 2026 midterm election. When asked about the importance of voting this year compared to past midterm elections, 58 percent of likely voters say it is more important, 39 percent say it is about as important as in past years, and only 2 percent say voting is less important to them. Californians are more likely to say that voting in the midterm is more important to them this year than they were in September 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2022/) (43%) and in September 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2018/) (52%). Today, Democratic likely voters (69%) are much more likely than Republicans (50%) and independents (45%) to say that voting in this midterm is more important this year. Majorities across the state’s regions say that voting in this midterm election is more important this year. Those who say they would vote for Democratic candidates (64%) are more likely than those supporting Republican candidates (49%) in their local House races to say that voting is more important to them this year than in past midterms.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We also gauged support for five state propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Fifty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute that authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 43 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (75% Democrats, 19% Republicans, 56% independents) and between homeowners and renters (49% to 72%). Half or more across the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that increases the state’s rainy day fund, approved by voters in 2014 to provide funding for economic downturns; 39 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (82% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 60% independents). Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 2 across age, education, gender, homeownership, and income groups and the state’s major regions.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-two percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute that repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 53 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (55% Democrats, 19% Republicans, 41% independents). Half or more would vote no across the state’s major regions.
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Thirty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment; 59 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 5 falls short of a majority across partisan groups (40% Democrats, 34% Republicans, 28% independents) and across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . Forty-three percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that increases the percentage of voters needed to approve local special taxes from a majority to two-thirds; 51 percent would vote no. Support varies across partisan groups (33% Democrats, 61% Republicans, 43% independents) and state regions (60% Central Valley; 50% Orange/San Diego; 43% Los Angeles; 35% Inland Empire; 32% San Francisco Bay Area).
When we asked likely voters which of the 14 state propositions they are most interested in, 9 percent chose one of the five legislative ballot measures (5% Proposition 1; 1% Proposition 2; 1% Proposition 4; 1% Proposition 5; 1% Proposition 43). Proposition 39 , also known as the California voter ID initiative , is an initiated constitutional amendment (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initiated_constitutional_amendment) in the state of California (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California) that on November 3, 2026, will be on the ballot. The initiative would amend the state constitution (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_California) to require the use of a government-issued ID for in-person voting, as well as the last four digits of a unique government-issued ID number when casting a mail-in ballot (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mail-in_ballot).
The amendment would also require the state of California to provide free voter ID cards that can be used to cast a ballot, and would enforce the maintenance of accurate voter registration lists by the secretary of state (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_secretary_of_state) and election officials. If approved, the amendment would make California the 37th U.S. state to require voter ID during elections, and the 10th U.S. state to support a voter ID ballot measure.
Background
[ edit (https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2026_California_Proposition_39&action=edit&section=1) ]
Currently, the state constitution (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_California) limits voting to U.S. citizens (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._citizens), though proof of citizenship (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_of_citizenship) is not required unless a voter has become a U.S. citizen less than 15 days before an election. During the voter registration process, individuals must provide a form of ID and attest that they are a U.S. citizen under penalty of perjury (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perjury). [ 1 ] California is one of only 14 U.S. states that does not require identification while voting on election day (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Election_Day_(United_States)). [ 2 ]
On April 24, 2026, state officials announced that the initiative had qualified for the November ballot after supporters submitted over 1.3 million signatures. [ 3 ] [ 4 ] [ 5 ]
Three other states – Nevada (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Nevada_Question_7), North Carolina (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_North_Carolina_Require_Voter_Identification_Amendment), and Oklahoma (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma) – will also see voter ID measures on their November 2026 ballots. [ 6 ]
Impact
[ edit (https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2026_California_Proposition_39&action=edit&section=2) ]
The initiative would amend the state constitution to enforce the use of government-issued ID while voting in-person, and the use of the last four digits of a government-issued ID number when voting by mail (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mail-in_ballot). [ 3 ] Additionally, it would mandate the maintenance of accurate voter registration lists by the secretary of state (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_secretary_of_state) and county election officials, and require the state of California to provide free ID cards upon request to voters casting a ballot. [ 3 ]
The voter ID initiative would also authorize the California legislature (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_legislature) to enact laws that would force compliance with the amendment, and permit citizens to seek judicial review if they feel the state of California or any county within it is failing to comply with the amendment. [ 7 ] Additionally, the state auditor (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_Auditor) would be required to publicly audit state and county compliance every second year. [ 7 ]

California Prop 39: What the voter ID measure may change & where it fits in the national battle
LAist's Jill Replogle shares what she’s learned from the author of Prop 39, its opponents and election experts.
This initiative would change California’s constitution to require voters to provide a government-issued ID when they cast a ballot. Mail-in voters would have to include the last four digits of their ID on the ballot envelope. The measure would also require election officials to use “best efforts,” using government data to verify that voters on registration rolls are U.S. citizens, and to report annually the percentage verified.
What’s at stake?
Voter ID. This would be a big change from how voting currently works in California.
Right now, election officials verify a voter’s identity when they register to vote. They also verify that the signature on a voter’s mail-in ballot matches the signature in their voter registration file.
But voters do not have to provide ID every time they cast a ballot.
Prop. 39 would change that and require voters to present a government-issued ID every time they vote.
The initiative would also shrink the long list of documents (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/regulations/hava_id_regs_from_barclays_3_3_06.pdf) the state currently accepts as proof of identity and residency for voting purposes. If Prop. 39 passes, only government-issued IDs, such as a driver’s license, passport, or state ID card, would be accepted.
The measure would require California to offer free state ID cards to eligible voters who lack another type of government-issued ID.
Official title on the ballot: Prop. 39: Prohibits citizens from voting unless they present government-issued identification
Language you will see: (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/index.htm)
Invalidates mail ballots that do not have last four digits of designated government-issued identification number written on envelope. Prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Fiscal Impact: Costs of between tens of millions of dollars and low hundreds of millions of dollars each year to implement new voting requirements.
What your vote means
A "yes" vote means: Voters would be required to present additional identifying information to elections officials each time they vote.
A "no" vote means: A voter’s identity would continue to be established with the voter’s signature.

Here's what voters need to know about the three seats up for election on the Pasadena Unified Board of Education.
Understanding Prop. 39
Currently, when someone registers to vote in California, they do not have to provide proof of citizenship. Rather, they have to check a box on their registration form attesting to being a U.S. citizen and California resident.
Lying on that form is a crime (perjury) punishable by fines and jail time.
Prop. 39 wouldn’t change that process.
What it would do is require election officials to make “best efforts” to verify the citizenship of people on voter registration rolls by cross-referencing their information against government data.
Why now?
According to a recent UC Berkeley poll (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/8hv8929c), just 22% of California Republicans surveyed have confidence in the election system, compared to 88% of Democrats. The two Republican legislators who proposed Prop. 39 see it as a step toward remedying that distrust.
President Donald Trump has also increasingly cast doubt on the integrity of elections across the U.S., including the claim that large numbers of noncitizens are voting. Efforts to find and prosecute noncitizen voters have thus far turned up few culprits (https://www.propublica.org/article/noncitizen-voting-trump-homeland-security-investigations).
But there have been a handful of recent cases in the news of noncitizens registering to vote, including a Honduran green card-holder who was charged with voter fraud (https://www.justice.gov/usao-cdca/pr/honduran-national-living-san-fernando-valley-arrested-federal-criminal-complaint) in August. Last year, an election integrity activist in Orange County was charged with fraud for registering and voting for her dog (https://laist.com/news/politics/dog-registered-to-vote-orange-county-redistricting-fight).
Here’s what supporters say
Supporters of Prop. 39 say requiring voter ID is a common sense reform to increase trust in the electoral process while maintaining voter conveniences including mail-in ballots. Supporters note that polling has found widespread support (https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2025/08/22/majority-of-americans-continue-to-back-expanded-early-voting-voting-by-mail-voter-id/) for voter ID across political parties. They also say using a voter’s signature on their mail-in ballot to verify identity, as California currently does, delays election results and causes some valid voters to have their ballots rejected.
Notable supporters: California Republican Party, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, Republican gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton, U.S. Congressman Ken Calvert (CA-41), Republican state Senator. Tony Strickland (Huntington Beach), Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (San Diego).
Here’s what opponents say
Opponents of Prop. 39 note that documented voter fraud is extremely rare (https://electionfraud.heritage.org/). They say the initiative feeds into Trump’s false claims of widespread election fraud, and would unfairly shut out eligible voters who make simple mistakes, like mixing up their ID number when writing it on their ballot envelope. They also say the federal government’s current system for verifying state voters’ eligibility is prone to error (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/watch-out-false-voter-fraud-claims-fueled-save-program).
Notable opposition: California Democratic Party, UCLA Voting Rights Project, U.S. Senator Alex Padilla, California Labor Federation
Potential financial impact
The state Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates that implementing Prop. 39 could cost anywhere from tens of millions to several hundred million dollars. Read the full analysis here (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=39&year=2026).

State and local election officials would be required to make “best efforts,” using government records, to verify the U.S. citizenship of registered voters and report annually on the percentage verified in each county.

Proposition 39 would require anyone voting in person in California to present a government-issued ID, and those voting by mail ballot to include the last four digits of the government-issued ID number they provided when they registered to vote.
In-person voters without ID would be turned away, while mail ballots without an attached ID number that matches their registration would be rejected.

By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.mercurynews.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: November 2, 2026 at 2:39 PM PST | UPDATED: November 2, 2026 at 6:04 PM PST
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 39, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=39&year=2026), would require election officials to verify Californians’ U.S. citizenship and prohibit them from voting without a government-issued ID. It also creates other rules around the voting process and identity verification when voting in person vs. by mail and ongoing compliance checks.
Voting “yes” would mean that you need to present a government-issued ID to vote in person and if you’re voting by mail, you need to provide the last four digits of that ID.
Voting “no” means the process stays is it is — you don’t need to present an ID to vote and your citizenship is verified during the registration process.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Voter Identification, Citizenship Verification, and Registered Voter List Administration Initiative, see it as a common-sense solution to voter fraud and a way to boost confidence in our elections.
Opponents see it as an extension of the Republicans’ currently stalled SAVE America Act and Donald Trump’s unfounded assertion that he lost the 2020 election thanks to noncitizen voters. It is also seen as a way to reduce voter participation by making it harder to vote.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-39-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
How many illegal votes were cast in California’s last statewide election? I’m asking for a documented number, not an estimate of fraud you believe went undetected.
First, measuring fraud requires you to actually look for it and investigate it — neither of which is a priority of politicians right now in California. Second, whether you believe voter fraud is just a small problem or a big one, Prop. 39 is trying to solve a more serious and well-documented problem of public trust. A recent poll conducted by University of California, San Diego’s Center for Transparent and Trusted Elections showed 13% of Democratic voters have less confidence in elections than just two years ago — with 17% of Republicans and 16% of independent voters having less trust as well. Declining trust and confidence in elections is not a partisan problem — this is a democracy challenge that Prop. 39 fixes in a bipartisan way.

Of the documented cases, how many involved someone appearing at a polling place and impersonating another voter — the conduct that presenting ID in person would directly address?
First, your question incorrectly frames the problem Prop. 39 is trying to address — the dramatic decline in public trust in our elections. Polling consistently shows that a solid majority of Democratic, independent and Republican voters all say they would trust our elections more if we implemented Voter ID. Moreover, Prop. 39 will also ensure we improve identity verification for mail ballots by switching from the unreliable signature checks to the much easier four digits of a government ID.
Heritage describes its fraud database as a noncomprehensive “sampling” and makes no claim about the overall prevalence of fraud. Without comparing its selected cases with the billions of ballots cast, how can it establish that fraud is common enough to justify Prop. 39?
This question has now been answered twice above. You are missing the point of why Prop. 39 is needed — it is designed to improve public trust and confidence in our democracy. That is a big problem you seem to be ignoring here. With the polling showing declines in public trust — and support for reasonable voter ID requirements — why would you not want to implement Prop. 39 to improve trust and confidence in our elections?
California already establishes identity during registration and verifies mail-ballot signatures before counting them. What evidence shows these safeguards are failing often enough to require an additional check on every ballot?
First, Prop. 39 is about verifying identity when someone casts a ballot — not just when they register to vote. Second, a 2022 report by the Transparency Foundation showed an appalling lack of consistency in the signature checking process on mail-in ballots in many counties. Prop. 39 allows us to replace unreliable signature checks with an easier-to-use, four-digit PIN based on a government document of each voter’s choice.
The LAO estimates annual costs ranging from tens of millions to the low hundreds of millions of dollars. How many unlawful votes would Prop. 39 prevent each year, and what would taxpayers be paying per vote prevented?
The LAO cost estimate is wildly inaccurate and fails to account for the cost savings that would result by improving the accuracy of our voter rolls with saving on postage and printing of mail ballots. Prop. 39 will ultimately save money — while improving public trust and confidence in our democracy. Seems like a great return on investment.
The LAO says the measure could reduce registration among eligible voters who lack government-issued identification. How many eligible citizens is it acceptable to keep from voting to prevent one illegal vote?
This is absurd! Did requiring an ID to fly on an airplane reduce air traffic in the US? In states that have implemented voter ID, participation in voting has actually increased! Your question is grossly biased by falsely suggesting that citizens will be prevented from voting. Prop. 39 seeks to keep voting easy while improving identity checks in a balanced way to improve trust and confidence.
Prop. 39 requires “best efforts” to verify citizenship but does not define the term. Which government records are sufficiently complete and current to determine the citizenship of every registered voter?
First, it is not hard to define citizenship in the US — it is already well defined. Second, a variety of government databases exist to help election officials double check citizenship. That’s all Prop. 39 requires — which is why Prop. 39 is a balanced approach to implementing voter ID.
If government records cannot verify someone’s citizenship, does that person remain eligible to vote? If not, why should the government’s failure to find confirming information be treated as evidence that the person is ineligible?
Prop. 39 intentionally does not put any additional burdens on voters, which is why Prop. 39 specifically does not require that any voter provide documents to prove their citizenship to the government, as that is prohibited under current federal law. Instead Prop. 39 holds government officials accountable to double check citizenship using government databases.

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 39, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=39&year=2026), would require election officials to verify Californians’ U.S. citizenship and prohibit them from voting without a government-issued ID. It also creates other rules around the voting process and identity verification when voting in person vs. by mail and ongoing compliance checks.
Voting “yes” would mean that you need to present a government-issued ID to vote in person and if you’re voting by mail, you need to provide the last four digits of that ID.
Voting “no” means the process stays is it is — you don’t need to present an ID to vote and your citizenship is verified during the registration process.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Voter Identification, Citizenship Verification, and Registered Voter List Administration Initiative, see it as a common-sense solution to voter fraud and a way to boost confidence in our elections.
Opponents see it as an extension of the Republicans’ currently stalled SAVE America Act and Donald Trump’s unfounded assertion that he lost the 2020 election thanks to noncitizen voters. It is also seen as a way to reduce voter participation by making it harder to vote.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the Yes campaign, go here (https://wp.me/p7ShJJ-SXLk).
How many eligible Californians do you expect Prop. 39 would prevent from voting, and what evidence supports that?
No one knows exactly how many eligible Californians Prop. 39 would block from voting, but we know that extra, unnecessary ID requirements don’t affect everyone equally. In other states, similar rules have led to eligible voters having their ballots rejected because of missing, incorrect or mismatched ID info. When Texas rolled out similar mail-ballot ID rules, mail ballot rejections shot up to 12% (https://www.texastribune.org/2022/04/06/texas-mail-in-ballot-rejection-voting/) and the Brennan Center for Justice found that Black, Latino and Asian voters had their ballots rejected at higher rates than white voters for ID mistakes or omissions. Recent studies, including from the University of Maryland (https://cdce.umd.edu/sites/cdce.umd.edu/files/pubs/Voter%20ID%20survey%20Key%20Results%20June%202024.pdf), have also shown that Californians are significantly less likely to have a current ID if they are people of color, younger, lower-income or have a disability. When eligible voters are turned away or their valid ballots are rejected, they’re less likely to try to participate in future elections.

The state would provide a voter ID card at no cost to voters who request one. What barriers would remain for eligible voters?
Even if the voter ID card is free, plenty of hurdles remain. People still have to take time off work, arrange transportation and childcare, gather paperwork or pay fees to get copies of documents like birth certificates and deal with bureaucracy. For anyone with mobility issues, a tight schedule, limited financial resources or trouble accessing government offices, these steps can go from inconveniences, to challenges, and then become real barriers — and all to satisfy disproven election conspiracies. In short, just because something is free doesn’t mean it’s easy or accessible for everyone. Requiring the state to issue IDs just for voting, when our elections are already secure, pushes underrepresented voters further out of democracy and wastes a massive amount of taxpayer money.
In-person voters currently identify themselves by signing the voter roster, but the LAO says those signatures generally are not verified before ballots are counted. Is that adequate?
California already has a safe and accessible process to check that someone is registered and eligible to vote at the polls. Election officials verify the identity and eligibility of everyone in the voter registration database and regularly maintain and update those records using reliable sources, including DMV and Social Security records. Requiring in-person voters who have already been verified to provide name, address and a signature swearing under penalty of law that they are who they say they are ensures security without creating new barriers. The real question is whether adding another ID requirement would actually make our elections more secure, or just make it harder for people to vote. Prop. 39 offers no evidence that it makes elections safer, and a court held (https://www.courthousenews.com/california-judge-rules-voter-id-supporters-must-rewrite-ballot-arguments/) that imposing this “extra step” on voters certainly doesn’t make voting easier.
Evidence indicates that in-person impersonation is extremely rare. Does its rarity mean no additional precaution is warranted, even in an election decided by one or two votes?
We should only add new rules if they address an actual problem and the benefits outweigh the downsides for eligible voters. The conservative Heritage Foundation found (https://www.businessinsider.com/voter-election-fraud-statistics-rare-president-biden-trump-2020-2020-11) that between 2000 and 2020, out of 250 million votes cast by mail in the U.S., there were only 193 proven fraud cases. The Brennan Center also found that in-person voter impersonation is so rare that someone is more likely to be struck by lightning. These numbers show that our elections are already secure. Prop. 39 isn’t a precaution — it’s unnecessary and adds expensive bureaucratic barriers that could block millions of eligible Californians from voting. The twin goals of elections should always be expanding access to increase participation for eligible citizens and ensuring the will of the voter though secure and accurate procedures. We have the second goal covered in California; we should focus more on the first one.
Heritage’s database does not establish a fraud rate, but it documents proven election offenses. Which documented vulnerabilities do you believe California’s current system has not adequately addressed?
Every state, including California, has had rare and isolated cases of election misconduct, and those should be, and are, taken seriously. But a handful of cases — out of hundreds of millions of votes — doesn’t mean there’s a big flaw in the system. It means the system is working effectively to keep the number so dramatically low. California already has strong, well-researched and tested processes to keep voter rolls up to date, check registration information, prevent double voting or impersonation and audit ballots. If Prop. 39 is supposed to solve a real problem, that problem needs to be clearly defined and

last four digits of the government ID selected in the voter’s registration. What happens if an eligible voter transposes two digits, omits them, renews the ID or provides digits from a different valid ID?
Prop. 39 fixes a serious problem with the current mail-ballot verification process, which relies solely on signature matches — and some voters’ signatures have changed over the years and their ballots are being invalidated as a result. In the last election more than 100,000 mail ballots were rejected due to signature mismatches. Prop. 39 replaces that process with four digits from a government ID to ensure every eligible vote is counted — and allows a “curring” process if a voter transposes numbers to make sure every valid vote counts.
The proposition leaves the Legislature to decide which identifications qualify and what constitutes “best efforts” citizenship verification. Why should Californians amend their Constitution before knowing the rules that will determine whether their ballots are counted?
No, that is not true. Prop. 39’s reference to “best efforts” simply establishes the expectation that our county election offices do their best job in maintaining their voter rolls. The Legislature can help clarify that, but ultimately, Prop. 39 gives courts the authority to ensure proper compliance with the expectations voters are imposing to improve election management. California is currently not using widely accepted list management practices that are used in red and blue states across the country.
What elections in California over the last 100 years should be called into question because the number of illegal votes was officially found to be high enough to have swung the results?
This question is not relevant to the stated goal of Prop. 39 — which is to improve public trust and confidence in our democracy going forward. We are not engaging in conspiracy theories or accusations about stolen elections because that is exactly counter to our goal of restoring trust through widely supported bipartisan election integrity reforms.
What do opponents of Prop. 39 get most wrong?
Opponents of Prop. 39 falsely claim this is a Donald Trump scheme. Prop. 39 is absolutely not the same as Trump’s SAVE Act. Prop. 39 is the bipartisan alternative to implementing voter ID in a balanced way without burdens on voters — and with the singular goal of improving trust and confidence in our elections. We believe Prop. 39 will become the national model for how to get voter ID done in a bipartisan way, and California citizens need to lead the way where partisan politicians have failed us.

backed by evidence that current safeguards aren’t enough. Otherwise, it only creates new barriers for eligible voters, which compounds the real problem of low and unequal turnout by eligible voters in our democracy.
California currently verifies mail-ballot signatures. What is your objection to adding a match of four identification digits, assuming eligible voters receive notice and an opportunity to correct mistakes?
The problem is that Prop. 39 layers unnecessary stumbling blocks onto a process that’s already working, creating more ways for a legitimate mail ballot to get tossed out. California already checks signatures on mail ballots and gives people a chance to fix signature issues, and that’s in addition to the registration verification and ballot tracking the state does. Prop. 39 would require mail voters to “designate” a specific ID number to use for voting, remember potentially years later which form of ID they designated, and perfectly match the last digits of that number each time they vote. This means another hoop to jump through, and voters can easily get tripped up if they write the wrong digits or provide a signature but not the ID number. And Prop. 39 doesn’t provide a way for voters to fix these simple mistakes — or even receive notice — before their ballot is thrown out.
Citizenship is already required for federal, state and almost all California local elections. What is objectionable about asking officials to use government data to make “best efforts” to verify that registered voters are citizens?
Citizenship is already a voting requirement in the California Constitution. Anyone registering to vote must swear, under penalty of perjury, that they’re a U.S. citizen. California keeps a statewide registration system and regularly checks the rolls against reliable databases. Prop. 39 is adding another layer of “citizenship checks” that would mistakenly flag some naturalized citizens as noncitizens, especially since no comprehensive government database of U.S. citizenship exists. Recent ProPublica reporting on similar checks using Trump’s SAVE database revealed that this could yield an “ungodly” number of false positives (https://www.propublica.org/article/noncitizen-voting-trump-homeland-security-investigations). Prop. 39 would force a vague mandate on election workers who are already overworked and they’d have to repeat this wasteful and error-prone task annually. Before we add yet another verification layer, subject to mistake or political abuse, we need strong evidence that the current system isn’t working and that the new process won’t block eligible voters.
Prop. 39 does not specify that a voter must be removed merely because citizenship cannot be verified through government data. Are opponents distinguishing between what the measure expressly requires and what future implementing legislation might require?
Prop. 39 doesn’t mandate removing a voter just because their citizenship couldn’t be confirmed — but the concern is implementation. Experts agree that there is no complete, accurate list of who is and isn’t a U.S. citizen, which means any fishing expedition conducted because of Prop. 39 would result in error-filled reports. This fuels confusion, disinformation and mistrust in our elections, giving ammunition to bad actors who want eligible voters purged from the rolls. Prop. 39 also lets private actors sue elections officials, forcing underresourced local governments to choose between caving to demands for overly aggressive voter purges and spending taxpayer money to defend against frivolous litigation. Because so many details are left open, future changes or court cases could create new problems for voters flagged by the process. So, it’s not just about what’s written in Prop. 39; it’s also about the uncertainty it creates down the line.
The measure requires annual reporting of the percentage of registered voters whose citizenship has been verified and biennial state auditor reviews of state and county compliance. Do you oppose those requirements themselves, or primarily their cost and connection to the identification mandate?
We’re concerned about both. California already requires voters to swear they’re citizens and has proven systems to check registration information and keep the rolls up to date. Prop. 39 would add redundant, wasteful and potentially dangerous mandates to the work of our trusted and under-resourced elections officials without showing that the current system is broken. It would also require ongoing reporting and audits, which could cost state and local governments tens or even hundreds of millions of dollars each year, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office. We should be asking whether these costs actually solve a real problem before making taxpayers and county election officials pay the price.
If your objection is that Prop. 39 leaves critical protections to future legislation, would you support a narrower law that specifies broadly acceptable ID, provisional voting, advance notice and a guaranteed opportunity to correct errors? If not, is your objection to this measure’s drafting or to voter ID requirements generally?
The main issue is that Prop. 39’s new requirements would create unnecessary new hurdles for eligible voters and new ways to reject valid ballots, without offering any evidence that there’s a problem it would solve. Voter participation rates in the U.S. are already amongst the lowest for many industrialized countries. We also have concerns about how Prop. 39 is written since it leaves many important details to future laws, like which IDs would be accepted, whether mail voters would get notice or a chance to fix mistakes with their ID number, and what counts as “best efforts” for citizenship checks. The Legislative Analyst’s Office provided a large cost-estimate range because so much is left undefined in Prop. 39. Election laws should keep voting secure without making it harder for people who have the right to vote.
What do proponents of this get most wrong?
Proponents get two big things wrong. First, California’s elections are already safe and secure, with strong systems for checking voter registration and keeping the rolls accurate and up to date. Second, Prop. 39 would fundamentally change how we vote; more than 80% of Californians voted by mail in the 2024 presidential election. Prop. 39 would force those voters to add the last four digits of a specific ID number to their ballot envelope, creating the risk of ballot rejection for simple errors and exposing them to identity theft. It would add new ID requirements for in-person voters and subject all voters to repeated, faulty citizenship checks. This isn’t just a small administrative tweak; it’s a major change, backed by MAGA billionaires (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316461529.html) and demanded by President Trump, who called for it as a precondition for California receiving federal aid after the 2025 Southern California wildfires. That context matters here.

Would Prop 39 speed up or slow down California’s vote-counting?
By Sara DiNatale (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/sara-dinatale/) , Staff Writer Oct 11, 2026
Marion Gautier helps organize and count absentee and mail-in ballots at the San Francisco Department of Elections at City Hall on Nov. 6, 2019.
Gabrielle Lurie/S.F. Chronicle
Most of the conservatives who critique California’s election system have two separate complaints: They believe California’s vote-counting process is riddled with fraud, and they think the state takes far too long to count its votes. (Many say that the latter is evidence of the former.)
Backers of Proposition 39, a measure to implement voter ID requirements, say their plan will solve both issues. Experts, however, say the measure’s requirements would slow down, not speed up, vote-counting.
Chronicle endorsements: Editorial Board’s recommendations for 2026 election (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2026/california-sf-election-endorsements/)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 39 would require voters to show government-issued identification each time they cast a ballot in person. People who vote by mail would have to register a PIN that’s either the last four digits of their Social Security number or their driver’s license number. They could also request a free “voter ID” with a number on it. The number would need to be handwritten on the ballot envelope. Election offices would then have to check and verify the number. Critics say that means essentially 26 million people would have to reregister to vote across California.
The proposition’s cocreator, Assembly Member Carl DeMaio, R-San Diego, has cast Prop 39 as a simple and necessary change to fortify voters’ trust in state elections. During a May episode of his podcast, DeMaio said the measure’s requirement of a four-digit PIN would replace the signature verification process for the more than 80% of voters using mail-in ballots. He said that if Prop 39 becomes law, mail-in ballots would be processed “literally within 48 hours of them coming back.”
Meredith Shields, the press secretary for the Yes on 39 campaign, reiterated those claims in a statement on Friday, saying “providing a four-digit PIN when voting by mail, election officials will not have to match electronic signatures.”
But the measure does not contain any language about the PIN numbers usurping signature verification, which is codified in state law. That means the new handwritten PINs would be required and verified in addition to signatures, not in lieu of them, voting experts said.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
The state’s official voter guide lays out what a yes vote means: “Voters would be required to present additional identifying information to elections officials each time they vote” — language that suggests the PIN is an extra layer of verification, not a replacement.
“Voters can read the language of Prop 39 for themselves,” said Brittany Stonesifer, an attorney and voting rights advocate with nonprofit California Common Cause. “It would add additional requirements for mail ballots. It says nothing about removing the existing signature verification process.”
DeMaio suggested during his podcast that there would be a “scanning” system for the PIN numbers, but that would require infrastructure and technology that election offices don’t yet have.
“The notion that this will speed up the process is asinine,” said Stephen Richer, a Republican former recorder of Maricopa County, Ariz. “I don’t know how having an additional requirement could possibly make the process go faster.”
Richer said he broadly supports ID checks at polling places to verify that the person trying to vote matches the person recorded in the voter rolls. California doesn’t do that. Voters must present a government ID when they register to vote, but when voting in person they only must provide poll workers with their name and address, and sign a voter roster.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
“It would absolutely result in valid mail ballots being rejected, potentially at a high level, with no evidence that it would increase security,” Stonesifer said of the four-digit PIN numbers.
Assembly Member Gail Pellerin, D-Santa Cruz, who is the head of the Assembly Elections Committee and a former elections official, agrees. She told the Los Angeles Times (https://www.latimes.com/california/newsletter/2026-09-28/skelton-monday-politics-newsletter-voter-id) that under Prop 39, not only would some voters’ ballots be rejected by mistake but the measure would “absolutely” slow down counting.
Richer, Stonesifer, Pellerin and other voting experts largely agree signature verification is a secure and efficient way to vet mail-in ballots. Some election offices use software to quickly confirm a signature match and kick any questionable ones to workers who can pull up someone’s state signature history to see how it may have changed over time.
If the signature still looks odd, they notify the voter it needs to be fixed. California has a long window allowing ballot curing, which is a common criticism of the state’s lagging vote-tallying process. But legislation just signed into law by Gov. Gavin Newsom requires all counties to allow digital signature curing in order to speed the process.
Shields, the Prop 39 campaign spokesperson, said the measure would not only speed the process, but would conserve resources.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
“When Prop 39 passes, IDs will be free of charge and the verification and counting of ballots will be faster, more accurate, and will save election officials valuable time and resources,” she said.
The state’s nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, however, estimates the measure would cost the state and local governments tens of millions to hundreds of millions of dollars. Darius Kemp, the director of Common Cause California, said the measure would also take resources away from counties and clerks, impeding them from counting more quickly.
Pamela Smith, president of Verified Voting, a nonprofit focused on election security, said that if someone was so determined to cheat that they would spoof a signature, there’s no reason to believe they wouldn’t also pilfer a PIN. She, too, was wary that the measure would speed up the count.
“The costs to taxpayers associated with implementation are significant, which might not matter if this were a game changer for efficiency or security, but it is neither,” Smith said.
Prop 39 does not include a curing process for PIN codes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
“My mother has very interesting handwriting,” Rep. Lateefah Simon, D-Oakland, said during a Friday rally against Prop 39. “If, in fact, the registrar of voters cannot read her handwriting or her Social Security number ... what will happen to her ballot? It will be discarded.”
State Sen. Jesse Arreguín, D-Berkeley, also argued the measure will impede in-person voting.
“Repetitive ID checks under Prop 39 are not only unnecessary, they will slow our checking and create longer lines and delays for people to vote and make it harder for them to participate in their right to vote,” Arreguín said during the Friday rally in Oakland.
Stonesifer said funding more staffers in election offices — rather than implementing a new system to scan four-digit codes — would be a better way to speed up the counting process.
DeMaio and his critics do agree on one thing: They’re all encouraging voters to return their ballots early. One of the biggest factors that slows California’s tabulation is the surge of vote-by-mail ballots returned on Election Day.

Sara DiNatale covers politics and the impacts of the Trump administration’s policies on the Bay Area and California. She joined the Chronicle in 2025, after a decade reporting across the southern United States for the San Antonio Express-News, the Tampa Bay Times and Mississippi Today.
DiNatale was a recipient of the 2026 Pulitzer Prize for Explanatory Reporting for her role in the Chronicle’s “Burned” series, which showed how California’s largest insurers shortchange wildfire survivors, threatening the recovery and health of whole communities. She was also awarded a 2024 George Polk Award for her investigation on the Texas residential solar industry, which led Texas to adopt new state laws to regulate bad actors and scammers. Her reporting has been recognized by state and national awards, including from the Investigative Reporters and Editors, Society for Advancing Business Editing and Writing, Headliner Foundation, Best of the West and Bill Minor Prize for Investigative Reporting. Those are still about two to four times the pre-SB1 range of roughly 0.8% to 1.7%, so education alone didn't bring them back down. I'm now checking what even a 1 to 2 point increase would mean for California's roughly 13 million mail voters.

I'm now checking the recent California rejection figures, since the 2024 general rate looks to be around 0.6 to 0.9 percent, and reports cite about 150,000 mail ballots rejected in the June 2026 primary. I also want to compare how mail voting in Texas, limited mostly to older and disabled voters, differs from California's universal system.

I'm checking Cantoni and Pons's 2021 QJE study of strict voter ID laws from 2008 to 2018, which found no drop in registration or turnout overall or for any group, and no effect on fraud. I also want to see whether these laws changed public trust, since that's the strongest pro-ID argument and the evidence seems to show little effect there too.

I'm now checking whether perceptions of fraud line up with voter ID laws, starting with Ansolabehere and Persily's 2008 Harvard Law Review work, which found those perceptions weren't tied to whether a state had an ID law, and then looking for newer research from the Bipartisan Policy Center.
